Reviews.172836:
So here's the thing...

-This game isn't for everyone. It's absolutely a "Chill" experience, so if you're expecting a fast action game like COD or an easy builder like Minecraft, look elsewhere. It took a certain mind set to keep me playing beyond the 10+ hour mark (namely drunk and/or high).
-This game pretty much requires mods for the best experience (low flight, fast actions, SHUT UP!, as well as several graphics mods).
-This game is MUCH better now then it was at release. Yeah there are still bug aplenty (like the stupid way-point markers getting stuck on my screen or the annoying inability to view blueprints without a free slot) but for the most part you'll just be battling the sporadic FPS which for me is either a solid 30fps, 60fps or 14fps and random graphical glitches (who doesn't love invisible mountains?)
-THE GRIND... yeah you're gonna be grinding for everything, often, so if that's not your thing look elsewhere.
-The combat is meh at best. You've got special classes for both your starships as well as your multitool which confer special bonuses based on the class. A fighter class for your multitool will give higher damage bonuses then a mining class much like a fighter class starship will do higher damage than an explorer class. There are also different tiers (ranked C to S) which further increases the bonuses. All of this is great except while you can keep multiple ships, you can (as of yet) only keep one multitool. Which is very unfortunate as there are multiple weapon types each of which is unique (oddly there are weapon racks that you can place as a decoration but can't hold a multitool).
-THE GRIND... seriously, there's a lot of it and trying to find the exact planet, in the exact system, with the correct resource you need is sheer luck.

It might sound like I'm being very critical of this game (and I am) but that's only because I've come to like it so much. I've recently started replaying the game and the new updates since release have significantly improved the game. If it had released as it is now it would have been significantly more well received and if the next update is anywhere near as good as they say then I'm even more hyped. 

So, in conclusion:
If you want a game to simply chill, relax and explore then this is your game, but if you want a fast paced action game or in depth story driven RPG look elsewhere. 

Also photo mode is pretty amazing, and for the love of god let me rearrange my suit / ship / multitool upgrades without destroying them!!!

99% of you are expecting Elite: Dangerous. If you want Elite: Dangerous, go buy Elite: Dangerous. If you already have Elite: Dangerous, carry on playing Elite: Dangerous. If you haven't played Elite: Dangerous and want to explore a huge galaxy without or without your friends, trade all the goods, shoot all the things, buy all the upgrades, etc. then buy Elite: Dangerous. No Man's Sky is NOT Elite: Dangerous.

Still here? Okay, No Man's Sky isn't a game in the traditional sense. Think of it more of a chillout experience, the sort of thing you play during that downtime between "proper" games. The basic game loop is set up such that you can jump in for as little or as long as you like and still make some progress, but really sustained gaming sessions for hours/day/weeks on end will just drain your ability to enjoy NMS for what it is. You'll be doing a LOT of resource collecting. No, really, a TON of resource collecting. You'd better enjoy resource collecting, because that's what you do for about 90% of the game, all of which serve to push you to new star systems and new planets -- mostly windswept, desolate hellholes, but push closer to the center of the galaxy and you might (MIGHT!) finally get that lush forest with the stampeding dinosaurs you saw in the trailer.

Is it fun to play? Maybe... That all depends on your ability to ride the wave of grind and whether or not an aesthetic reward (the occasional beautiful vista) is enough of a reward. Hello Games, to their credit, have been politely ignoring the vitriol surrounding the game and have pushed out a number of updates that add some interesting features, including base building for the sandboxers and new land vehicles for the explorers. It's not quite enough to push NMS into the realms of a bona fide sandbox experience to rival Minecraft, nor is there anything vaguely resembling a triple-A gaming experience on offer (which makes that $60 price tag, still there a year after release, nothing short of ridiculous), but if you can wait for a sale and want something you can dip in and out of while occupying your brain with something else (maybe your favorite gaming podcast) then by all means give it a whirl.

I know I'm coming to this game after several major updates, and even then, I can see why a lot of people might not enjoy it.  It's very slow paced, and there are some systems that could use a little more work.  But to me, No Man's Sky is just blissful.  It's by turns exhilarating in its vastness, yet gorgeously relaxing to just bum around in.  The worlds I've seen have been incredibly beautiful; from lush forests and tundra, to the bleakest, barren, poisonous rocks, they've all been an absolute pleasure to explore.  The spaces between things don't make the game boring to me, they make it immersive, and render each new discovery something special.  As a fan of games like Dear Esther and Abzu, this is a simple delight, yet one so grand in scale, and with far more gameplay possibilities than those games, now with base building as well as resource gathering, crafting, trading etc. that I could lose myself in it for a long, long time to come.

This is the first time I've written a Steam review, and I felt compelled to do it because of how much scorn has been poured on this game, and how much I love it.  Sony may have marketted No Man's Sky poorly, but Hello Games have created something wonderful here, that both needs and deserves the support of its players.  I'd be sad to see their future plans not come to fruition because of a rough launch and a reactionary public.

Realistically, I guess I couldn't recommend this game to just anyone, but to people like me, I can't recommend it strongly enough.

The people that are complaining about the gameplay and how boring it is clearly do not understand the game. There is way more than 2 hours of content. The bases do actually offer you quests and things to do to get new tech. There is no best ship/best multi tool in the game. People just don't get it. That is fine, this game is not for everyone. If you are looking for a chill experience where you can explore a beautiful universe, solve puzzles, learn about the different races- this is the game for you. If you are looking for a challenging experience definitely try permadeath. It is really challenging; one of the more difficult survival games to get a good foothold in if you are not very experienced with the game. 

There are no bad planets in the universe. Yes lots are trying to kill you, Yes, some have no resources to get(this is rare though; like really rare), yes, some have crazy sentinels that will shot you on site. All of these are problems that can be solved through game mechanics and progressing through tech; it's not because the planet sucks, you do; you just may not be outfitted to survive efficiently in that environment. Just grab your stuff and move on, You are not missing anything. There are a bunch of planets to visit, more than we could ever see.  Just because this one you just landed on is not perfect does not mean that there is not a perfect(to you) one out there... 

This is a slow roll type of game, and people trying to rush through a game that has no end should not leave comments/reviews... It is really idiotic when you actually think about... Do you want to take advice from an idiot? 

All of that being said:

The programming is sub par and it is way overpriced. It plays like a pre-release and a not finished game. That being said, they are still working on it; so hope is not misplaced.

There are lots of things that need to be addressed and frankly after a year of being released should have been fixed(at least on the PC side). Really no exit from mode select?... Lazy or don't know how?  It is blatantly obvious that HG made the game for console then were like we can so make a PC port, game works in PC, awesome, done. The controls are awful for PC, this can be fixed with mods and whatnot but, frankly HG should not be filling holes with 3rd party content/fixes/mods when they made as much money as they did off the initial hype of the game.

The UI will piss you off for the first few hours of game play and occasionally every so often afterwards. 

In my opinion the game is about finding something worthy of taking a screenshot of. This happens a lot, as the game is beautiful, but every so often you will find a spot where ship, planet/moon, mountains just line up in a way that makes an epic photo.

The player community that loves this game is truely amazing. I recommend the game just on that merit; they will save this game. 

If you need help or tips hit me up on steam or twitch.tv/ipreferpi.
Cheers and thanks for reading.
Reviews.172952:
I have been playing this game since release, and 1 year on, the game has changed drastically, The majority of negative reviews left about this game are from people who didn't understand what this game was going to be. This game is supposed to be an exploration game, as opposed to an epic space shooter with loads of epic stuff happening. 

This game is good at what it was made for, an endless deep space exploration game. 
Though I love this game and have made over 100 YouTube videos on this since October 2017 (now July 2017), It still needs updates and improvement. After exploring over 200 in game planets for at least 30mins each, You start to be able to see paterns and how the world generation works. Which is why I believe that, as you play the game, the world generation should change and adapt around you.

The animal situation is my least favorite part of the game. 
Fistly, Animals are pretty dull. they all look fairly similar, the potential this game has to invent new sorts of animals, rather than 4 legged deers. Plus the reward for finding all the species of animals on a planet is next to pointless. As when farming was introduced, all you have to do (with the right setup) is wait for 20mins, farm, then sell and you will get much more than you would from exploring a planet. There needs to be a bigger reward to treat players for finding everything.

The game engine isn't the best, at times it feels clunky and just overall a bit eh. but with future updates, this won't become a problem.

The potential this game has is incredible. Please Hello Games, keep updating the game in as many ways you can. to make this game an even more incredible experience.

Reviews.172963:
This game is a perfect example of how you shouldn't trust blindly in the masses' opinion. For me, at least.

I'll preface this short review by saying that I got bored after 1 hour and complained about it to my friends. The game was bland and crashed a lot at first, nothing special really happened.

But then I gave it a second chance and I started looking into it a little more. Learning the languages seemed to affect very little but it's actually really fun; crafting the next best thing is the classic progression system that everybody loves and roaming around the planets on your exocrafts, shooting stuff and making profits is everything a gamer dreams of in a sandbox. I speak for myself.

There's a lot to do for at least the 25 hours I've played. I've been doing quests, exploring planets and identifying animals and plants (the true sandbox experience), and I haven't even scratched the surface on spaceships or more importantly, base-building. I honestly don't see what's not to like about all of this in a sandbox game. And maybe that's the key: people seem to forget this is a sandbox game and that sandbox games don't have endless hours of objectives to do. You make your own fun. Just like in Minecraft, Terraria, Garry's Mod or any game of the sort.

The only negative aspects I have to say about this game is that there are a few bugs, a few crashes and the exocraft vehicles, although fun, are kind of irrelevant. Their purpose turns obsolete with inventory expansions, advanced mining tools and for fast travelling... Why not just take the ship? They're great for finding ruins and that's about it.

For a sandbox experience? 8/10. It's not incredibly groundbreaking but it is incredibily fun. Give it a shot and remember that the masses also think Justin Bieber is a good singer.

[h1]Short version[/h1]

[b]Get it if:[/b]

[list][*]you loved subnautica and wanted endless biomes to explore
[*]you like taking screenshots of awesome scenery
[*]you want a game to relax and fuck around without goals and storylines
[*]you like to play modded games
[*]you don't mind grinding, or you like playing in creative mode
[*]you used to read sci-fi novels as a kid, dreaming about visiting all those awesome places depicted on the covers
[*]you want a game to play with your kids[/list]

[b]Don't get it if:[/b]

[list][*]you want to do speedruns, or you tend to rush games
[*]you want multiplayer or coop
[*]you want a shooter
[*]you want a flight simulator and dogfights
[*]you want a realistic space sim
[*]you want to trade and like complex, well fleshed-out economic systems
[*]you want quests and goals
[*]your rig isn't very powerful and you can't tolerate low fps/graphic settings[/list]

[h1]Long version[/h1]

The best definition of this game I ever found is this one:

[url=https://steamcommunity.com/app/275850/discussions/0/135511027320764952/#c1458454827733523447][quote=SteveGamingFR]I like to describe No man's sky like a child who's saying "..and I'm gonna have a spaceship, and I'm gonna visit some weird planets, and I'm gonna find strange things and animals, and I'm gonna kill the pirates who wants my things pew pew pew! And with all my money I will buy the biggest ship in the universe and some cool space cars and build a huge base so I can grow plants!".[/quote][/url]

The gameplay is slow, grindy and - for some people - not very satisfying. You don't get a sense of achievement from the tasks the game gives you, but you get it from the goals you set for yourself. Finding an animal looking like this or that, finding a planet with those exact colors to set your base on, a new cool-looking ship with better class/inventory and so on.

Many people still talk about lies. Personally I was full on the hype train, I preordered, paid full price and I'm absolutely satisfied with the game. I never thought some things were in the game (like multiplayer... c'mon, Sean said many times before release that this was NOT a multiplayer game, and even Steam labelled it as a single player game) and even if I was bummed about some of the stuff that was shown in the trailers and didn't make it to final release I then realized that having all those things wouldn't make a huge difference, if at all, in terms of gameplay. Many of those missing features (like sandworms, huge fauna interacting with the environment etc) would be just another cool addition to the scenery, while stuff like realistic flight, planet rotation and things like that would just make the game annoying for me, adding a layer of complexity and challenge that I don't really want in my relax-and-unwind game.

Sure the game has some flaws, but many of them have been solved by 1.1 and 1.2 updates, and many others can get fixed using mods.

There's an awesome modding community for NMS. Simply adding Megaliths, Constructs, Space Dream and Fast Actions will make a huge difference if your goal is exploring and finding weird, fascinating new planets and scenery (and you're annoyed by that stupid click-and-hold thing). One can find mods for everything: shaders, content, ships, flight mechanics... plenty of stuff to make the game even more awesome than it is.

The two updates released after launch added lots of new content: basebuilding and exocrafts are awesome toys if you like to build and run around a planet in a tiny indestructible car, and the many quests you need to finish to get all the blueprints will give you several hours of grinding towards your goal. The nice thing tho is that you don't need to do them: sometimes I get bored of searching that damn rigogen everywhere I will just stop and start exploring aimlessly, or follow the atlas path, or go back to my base to build a new room, or whatever, and then I will go back to the quest or stumble on what I was searching for while doing something completely different. After 90 hours since release I didn't finish all the quests yet, and I still have only 1 of the 19 millions I'd need to buy a freighter.

Apparently, the 1.3 update will roll out in the near future and it's rumored it will be a big one, Hello Games has been doing an ARG to promote it and everyone's talking about it. When it will roll out I will update my review.

Would I buy this game again? Yes. Would I suggest it to my friends? Absolutely. But I do realize it is not a game for everyone, so be careful and watch some (RECENT) gameplay videos and read reviews before buying it, maybe even try it out if you know someone who already owns it: it could be your piece of cake or you could hate it.

Reviews.173055:
[h1]The Good Stuff:[/h1] 

I waited a long time to post this review. I will just start off by saying that the game in it's current state is certainly how it should have been released from the start, but hey, it's a much fuller package now. That can only be considered a good thing for someone just coming in for their first time. This is a great game for the Sci-fi Space / Exploration / Survival category. It's unlimited in where you can go and at times (depending on where you end up), can produce some absolutely breathtaking scenery.  It's a cool reality in the sense that you can spend literally hours exploring a single moon, or warping from star system to star system. The base building has plenty of options for the engineer in you to make your own masterpiece. All the while, you're assembling a crew of specialists, questing for upgrades on everything, and conducting business with a Star Base while your whole Freight (and your 2nd mobile base) orbits the planet or station. Graphically it's pretty well done, and the soundtrack is good as well.     


[h1]Not so Good Stuff:[/h1] 

Well, it's not that bad of a list based on my observation. Bear in mind that this game is in a genre very similar to the likes of Subnautica, Planet Nomads, Oasiris, Elite Dangerous, etc... With that said, It has it's strengths and weaknesses compared to it's peers. They all do. For example, Elite Dangerous (played on PS4) has a great space flight and combat experience but blows at everything else. Space combat in No Man's Sky is satisfying but also too lacking in the amount compared to it's counterparts. One can argue that it represents the vast loneliness and emptiness of space. Depends on who likes what. It is more eventful depending on the mode and difficulty setting you role with, but still could be more complete. Last but not least.... Multiplayer would have been nice since they did say it was going to be available before launch, but in hindsight, a lot of these survival games are meant to be a single player experience anyway. 

[h1]Verdict:[/h1]

It's a great game to pass the time and burn up some hours when all of your gaming buddies are busy. The base crafting and lust for enchanced equipment will keep you tied up till the sun rises. TLDR: Great game after Pathfinder and Foundations update added more to do.  Worth a purchase if it is on sale.

My hours played are incorrect since I only recently purchased the PC version of NMS.  I have roughly 300 hours played total between the PS4 and PC.  I will admit that I jumped on the hype wagon early on with NMS and while I enjoyed it on the PS4 I quit playing after about 40 hours out of boredom.  The two updates that have happend since have done a lot to increase the playability of the game, and has been the main driver I have came back to the game last month and played as much as I have.  I have also felt the quality of the game to be improved so much that I took advantage of the Steam Summer Sale to purchase it for my PC.

Graphicaly the game runs very well on my rig.  If you run SLI you will have to force multiple GPU's in your profile.  So far I have had no problems except for when I first load in, my fps drops from my hardcapped 90 to 5fps while the cinematic letterbox is displaying.  This only happens with SLI forced and only on the initial loading of my save.

The Pathfinder and Foundations updates have introduced a few more survival mechanics that were sorely missing in the initial release, namely Vehicles and Base Building, as well as updates to the crafting system which includes many new pieces of tech for your multi-tools and ships.  Also, advanced difficulty levels, including PERMADEATH have been introduced.  There is also a creative mode that is great for experiementing on base designs or just letting your younger children have a good time hunting "dinosaurs".

While some of the complaints from the early game are still present, they do not seem as noticable as before.  There seems to be much more variety in the planets I am encountering on both platforms then there was at first release, but about a third of the planets seem to be planets I've encountered before.  

Also still missing is any true multiplayer aspect.  While one can join the Hub Community and settle near worlds actively settled by others as well, you will never see these other players or interact with them save for the odd message module dropped by their base.  While it is rumored that Patch 1.3 will include full multiplayer, I will personally not count on that happening, though I hope to be surprised.

Unless 1.3 adds many upgrades and surprises, at this point I would reccomend buying this game while it is on sale.

Note: Dickhead comments will be killed. Read the fn review first.

[h1]PREFACE[/h1]
In a world of knee-jerk, downvote mentality displayed by so many bad-tempered morons it's unfortunate that any genuine review has to be prefaced with an explanation. I'm not sure why I'm bothering really because the aforementioned morons will neither read nor care for the preface, and this will get downed purely because I recommend this game - and I do, PROVIDED the points I raise are heeded.

[b]This review is for those that want a serious (albeit tongue-in-cheek) "I played this for 200+ hours" synopsis so you can balance the silliness of the review system to what you can actually expect.[/b]

..oo00oo..

Silky: Art. Exploration. Potential.
Rough: Purpose.

[h1]No Mans' Sky[/h1]
It must be said that this game attempted to launch into "mainstream" (whoever that is) and landed in "niche". There's enough said about the original launch and subsequent crash and burn to fill 2 universes... However, the 2 updates and a rather intriguing bit of hype for another significant update (which may be old news by the time you read this), has made an attempt to re-enter the void we call "space games".

[h1][i]The one thing that's [b]important[/b] - and make no mistake here - is without a serious exploration/discovery/ ♥2grind attitude it's going to be hard to enjoy this game. Without this attitude, the "finish" is limited to rushing to the "centre of the galaxy", getting all gushy about your achievement... and playing something else.[/i][/h1]

With that said...

On my very first "normal" play, I was completely and utterly lost as to what to do on a bloody cold miserable planet that was somehere in the middle of somewhere, one among millions of possible planets (apparently). I had up to this point annoyed the hell out of some botty-droney things, got killed lots, froze to death and filled my inventory with lots of unknown purpose goodies. After dying for the 10th time, I simply respawned again, replete with a nice little "grave" to collect my stuff. So far so good. This is not terminal. 

(note there is  "permadeath" mode - do NOT start there. Do NOT start in "survival" mode - 1 save, twice the difficulty. Suggest you don't start in "creative" mode either unless you're Bob the Builder, you won't learn what you need to know... Be "normal", like the rest of us.)

Without too much in the way of handholding, I managed to repair my ship and launched victoriously into the void. I could now see a "station" and it was obvious I had to go there. I pressed the combo of keys I was expected to press and whizzed across the gap to be snapped up nicely by the "docking beam" before being guided (on auto) to a shiney obsidian like flight deck.  (nope, NOT like Elite Dangerous at all.)

Having already jumped out (where auto save kicked in) I ran up the ramp (wheelchair access? Wow!) to the control centre. I opened the door and hello? Theres 2 or 3 ugly looking frog like dudes called "Geks", an ugly SOB called a "Vy'keen" and some glittery droid like dude from the "Korvax". They're all sitting around with their faces buried in their comms' devices (iPads?) like teenagers at a coffee shop.

(Have you ever come across a group of teens at a Cafe' Bar, nothing in front of them, taking up the seating, "talking" to each other across the table... using their freakin' phones? Yup, that's what it looks like.)

Anyway, after having a chat and realising they couldn't help me (yet) and I couldn't give them what they wanted (yet) I sauntered over to this "Galactic Trading" thingie. Saw 2 buttons called "Sell some stuff" and "Buy some stuff". So I sold some stuff and bought some stuff. (and the list of "stuff" in NMS can best be described by saying... think Sheldon Cooper. There's more "iums" in NMS than English... as you will find out). 

Since everything looked done, (well, no-one had anything more to divulge) I ran back down to my ship and promptly launched back out into space.. and got nailed by some pirate in 20 seconds because I had "valuable cargo". I don't know what I bought that was valuable but I'm guessing he needed it more than I didn't. While I was dying I'm getting all kinds of messages about recharging this and that (with, ironically, the stuff I sold to buy the shiney thing the pirate wanted so I suppose I only had myself to blame). After respawning back on the flight deck, I popped my head out again, sans everything, and hello? A grave. By now, I knew what I had to do so I flew over and got my stuff back.

This btw is in the first 30 minutes.. BUT... within this 30 minutes I had learned to survive, learned what not to do with those drones around, learned to fix my ship, fly my ship, get to and land at some places, talk to people (people?) and that none of this was going to be as simple as I thought. That's not a bad tutorial really. 

And here begins the gist of it.....

200 hours later I'm sitting here in my base, I just left my freighter (that cost $15m) in space. (I only just found an awesome S class fighter that had crashed and had to get it back to the freighter for repair. Didn't need that shuttle I left behind anyway.).

Anyway... my base is growing stuff to make explosives (so I can dig a tunnel to get to the emeril deposits) with a combination of "feverium" (another "ium") and "coprite" (cough.... animal poo). I'm only now able to do this after I finished meeting Polo & Nada (at the Atlas Anomaly in the system I am in which was pointed out to me after visiting my 3rd Atlas Interface 5 systems ago) and getting the TAU class blueprint (it goes well with the SIGMA upgrade for red systems don't you think?) I needed to travel to a green system,  where I got veridium to give to my agricultural assistant (or was that my scientist?) so I could grow feverium in my biospheres, that is made of glass, which I make with coryzagen, whcih I get from the same planet I get my rigogen, which I get under the sea using my exocraft, no, not the Colossus or Nomad exocraft, the other one.

My list of things to do include finding (or buying) the materials I need to add the 3 upgrades (on my 24 slot multitool) I now have the blueprints for, the latest having been secured from a Korvak that was sitting in an outpost that I scanned with my Signal Booster in between getting shot by drones who are really annoyed at me for landing on their green and fluorescent pink planet, replete with 12 different animals, some really big ones wanting to eat me (or sometimes really little ones who want to chew my ankles).

(Excuse me a minute... I just saw the cutest little bear. Or I think it was a bear... it was maybe 2 feet tall, pointy little ears, bear face, Mc'Donalds physique... Oh wait. That coyote looking cat/dinosaur thing just killed it. nvm)

Anyway, where was I? Ohhh... look. Tell you what. Just play it.

8/10 - if they keep adding updates... even slowly.

[h1]A GOOD buy only if what I wrote about, that deliberate rush of badly formed paragraphs, makes sense. Heed not what I say and it'll be One Man Cry. [/h1]

At $60, I would WAIT. At $24, which was my buy trigger, pretty easy to justify. Damn that bear was cute.....

PS: In my 2 line tl;dr analysis under the heading "Rough", the "purpose" of NMS is non-existent. It's just not there. The long and the short is there is NO reason to play unless you enjoy exploring, building and discovering for the sake of it. There's certainly underpinning "lore" but nothing really matters if you don't bother with any of it. Did Hello Game leave this incomplete? Is there more to come? If you're looking for an eye watering storyline to follow, to guide your path through the cosmos, the answer has to be a plain, unequivocable no.

This game was so full of controversy and butthurt I waited until it was on a -66% sale before I purchased it. I fully understand why people are upset if they paid like 60USD for this game, because it it definitively doesn't have nearly enough content to justify such a ridiculous price tag. But for 20USD I definitively feel its worth it. I've spent ~50 hours exploring, mining, building a few bases, buying a bunch of ships, and I've enjoyed it a lot. It has a visually beautiful and stunning universe, and in the first few hours of the game you always feel there's something new to see over the horizon. It feels quite magical, to be honest.

However... after a while you start to realize the universe is very monotone, and the same few game elements keeps repeating endlessly over and over. It feels stale. Very stale.  There's simply not enough variations and randomness to make it feel "endless". When you jump to a new star system, it's more like you're just resetting and starting over again. It doesn't feel like you're jumping to a brand new and fresh system. It's just recycled and jumbled around, with a new color palette. And the alien species are too few, which is very sad. Why not have more of them to create some diversity? 

It supports both mouse/keyboard and a gamepad controller. You can easily switch between them, and there's no need to adjust anything in the options to activate/deactivate if you're like me and keep switching every 10 minutes. The flight controls are utter horrible, and it's almost like the developer never played any flight (simulator) game in their life. It's pretty hopeless, and infuriating at times, but after a few hours you (un)learn and adjust your behaviour accordingly. 

The galaxy navigation map is another element that will infuriate all players, But after a while you unlearn all your years of gaming interface experience and go along on its backwards and counterintuitive controls. 

Is it worth 20USD? Well, yes. Will it give you a few hours of enjoyable gameplay? Definitively. Replay value beyond those first 30-50 hours of gameplay? None.

TL:DR.  
7.5/10.  
GOOD: Nice graphics, extremely addicitive gameplay, satisfying base building, and seamless transitions.  BAD:  No HOTAS or head tracking support (3rd party options available but still not great).  Terrible UI port from console (if you don't use a gamepad).  Pretty basic procedural generation of planets: they become same very fast (even though it's quite addicting).

Bought in the 2017 Steam sale like so many others.  Been playing Elite:Dangerous since Beta and dipping in and out of Star Citizen testing with some friends for a few years as reference.  Have been pleasantly surprised by the game so far.  Myself and a few other Rock Rats from ED have tried it out and have logged over 400hrs combined.  

Pros:
- Immersive gameplay
- Addictive gameplay (just one more planet discovery...)
- Relatively seamless transitions between planets and space
- Base building click-to-block is easy and intuitive
- Nice looking vistas.
- Nice simple storyline to follow.

Cons:
- UI is a very poor port from console to PC. Click and hold action on primary button is incredibly annoying.  Poor ability to remap keys in options menu. No native ability to remap gamepad right joystick (head look) with kb/m or some Exocraft functions.
- No native HOTAS support. Can use X360Ce to make Thrustmaster T16000 work but still ugly.
- No head tracking support at all.  Can make some USB options sort of work but it's not worth it.
- Planets quickly become the same between systems.

I didn't preorder NMS, because preordering a game has no benefits. You can see what happens when people preorder games in the countless amount of useless and toxic reviews here on steam.

Having played NMS for around 40h, I can say that there is a game in there, but it feels shallow and too much of a grind to me. 

In a nutshell, you fly around the procedural generated universe, cataloging flora and fauna for a credit reward on completion of a planet. This seems pointless after a while to me, because once you've seen all the different types of planets, you've seen them all. 

Pick a planet and make it it your home base is quite fun, but that goes out the window, once you realize that all you do is gathering resources, which at the beginning, is quite tedious in itself. 

After 40h I'm now at a point where credits aren't an issue anymore and my progress is only blocked by time (waiting for resources to be ready to be collected from my farm and mining units). I don't see the point of continuing playing the game. I beat it, so to speak. 

The fun here is to overcome the challenges. Built a base, create a source of income, find the largest ship. Problem is, there's nothing to do with it really. And that's my main issue with the game. There is a promise here that all the exploring and grinding for resources will pay off, but it never does, because at the point of the game where you're "rich" the game has peaked already. I realized this roughly after my 40h with the game and felt mislead. 

Atmosphere is great and controls feel solid to me. Performance and stability are a mess. 
Can't recommend this for $60. Game stays quite behind its potential.

Sometimes NMS feels a bit like a blend of Elite, Spore and Subnautica, if you can imagine such a thing.

Mind, this is not Star Citizen or Elite Dangerous. It is nowhere near as deep, and the gameplay has been brutally dumbed down to suit console players. The flight mechanics in particular can be painful as the terrain avoidance and "assisted" speed and attitude control makes precision flying and landing all but impossible. The HUD pitch ladder doesn't even come close to a proper readout. There are also some inexplicable UI limitations like the fact that items cannot be tranferred directly between your exosuit (=backback) and your exocraft (=rover) but must go via the starship cargo hold. Items can be transferred TO your starship from anywhere, but to transfer FROM your starship it must be in close proximity. These are just the most obvious ones.

This comes on top of a fair number of bugs, like randomly getting ejected several hundred meters out of your exocraft when simply trying to get out, the "pulse drive" autopilot occasionally going haywire, or the base construction tool randomly getting stuck in color/material mode forcing a restart of the game. I guess desperately adding new features that should have been in the game at launch must have given the QA dept a bit of a backlog.

The resources in the game are worth an entire article, suffice to say that some strange design decisions have been made.  As an example, the production of glass would in most games require some form of sand. In NMS you need to find a world with oceans and free dive for an ultra rare plant that can only be spotted during the night to pluck its "fruit". Uranium, on the other hand, can be found in the form of red crystals standing 1 meter tall just about anywhere you go. This means you will be flying thousands of light years and spend several hours in order to produce a single pane of glass, while fueling your starship can literally be done with your bare hands.

Some may find the actual exploration to be a bit tedious and repetitive, in which case a game firmly about exploration clearly isn't for you and you should go look for something else. So, after all this, how can I still recommend this game? Personally, I find the gameplay to be forgiving, relaxing and fun, even addictive. If you care for lore, there's a nicely written story line waiting for you to follow, but there's absolutely no pressure and you can do so at your own leisure.

Despite the exaggerated and out of control hype at launch time, I always believed in the technical potential of No Man's Sky. Although I liked the product proposal, even at the troubled launch, I still did not see any reason to buy it. It was, as its creators said, a beautiful canvas full of possibilities. But it was not "there" yet. 

Today, after two massive updates, the commitment of HG in improving his product is pretty visible. The community also matured a lot in the period, and began to rediscover the positive aspects of NMS. So, after a long wait, I decided to invest and test the game. 

In its current state, with the addition of new game modes and several new mechanics, No Man Sky is a lot of fun if you're looking for EXPLORATION, COLLECTION OF RESOURCES and a RELAXING EXPERIENCE. Do not come looking for an infinite procedural MMORPG. You will be disappointed. This is not the purpose of the game, and perhaps that is what many critics expected at the time of launch. Hence the widespread disappointment. 

New updates are expected regularly. By the time I write this review, a massive "ARG" creates a new, healthy hype around an upcoming update, probably in August. Following this alternative reality game is a lot of fun by itself :) 

Anyway, manage your expectations, and have fun with an unique game with vast potential. But don’t worry about the future. If you like the three pillars I´ve quoted up there, NMS is already on a very good point. And, as it seems, it only tends to improve.

The negative reviews are largely based on a highly warped expectation of what this "game" was supposed to be.
This honestly isn't even best described as a game. It's more of a toy. Think Spore, but focused on exploration from a ground level, first person pov. In the same way that Spore, Sim City, and Sims titles fail to have an interesting end game or goal, so does this. It's a strange generative universe with odd things to stumble upon. Unlike Sims games, though, it's not even really built to "entertain". This is a very "hard sci-fi" kind of game. The interest here is in pondering the nature of this artificial universe and soaking in a very specific kind of tone that isn't present in sci-fi much these days. It has no grit, very little conflict, and what few "characters" exist aren't really interested in getting to know you or vice-versa. There is no "adventure" to be had here, nor is this supposed to be Space Minecraft.
Another way to think of this is as a super-massive, sci-fi version of Proteus. I recommend you approach this game in the same way. If you didn't enjoy Proteus, you have no reason to expect enjoying this. Expect little in the way of guidance on how to have fun or instructions telling you what's worth accomplishing. This is very much like *actually* exploring the endless cosmos. Sometimes there just isn't much of interest, and on occasion you see something neat and interesting. If you liked Proteus and wish it had more weird, abstract, 70's scifi qualities, then you may be interested in checking this out. Or if you just like strange things and want to encourage the creation of more odd, unique games in the future.

The fact this game is still running mostly negative reviews is heartbreaking.

I have 50 hours into this game. I was convinced almost instantly that this game was amazing. I only obtained it recently after alot of patching if I understand correctly. However, patched up; it's now ready to rock. I will make this short and sweet.

- Top 3 Pros - 

- Endless - 
This game is ridiculously huge. Something that everyone hated on them so bad. This game is simply a pioneer. Sandbox is the best description with the endlessly generated worlds and events. There is always something there, albeit minute or huge.

- Discovery - 
Discovering the next class of ship or next planet or next galaxy or next species or.... You get the picture. Granted you can see some repetition but its always different to some level. Even if the species has a tiny set of wings. I mean, I've got to witness flying whales that fed on birds! 

- Simplicity -
This appeals to many gamers that do not want some complicated UI or endless customization options to make it comfortable. Smooth transitions into the atmosphere, space combat, experience small level politics, Warping to new universe. Even the story delivery in dialog is short, simple and still captivating.

- Top 3 Cons -

- NPC engagment -
The NPC engagment is there. There is just nothing in depth. A diplomacy meter is used to allow purchasing of Blueprints to progress your character. Which is great. Otherwise, there are limited options.

- ...Simplicity... -
Even the space stations are a little dry. I am okay with reciprocity, makes sense when spreading an empire over the billions of galaxies. However, it's empty. Or repetitive.

- Guide -
The map and large scale navigation for something this HUGE should be direct and easy. It lacks in markings and capability unless using the discoveries box. The story directs you and the main goal of the galaxy directs you. What happens when you begin creating your own map out, making money of mining and needing to note your routes easier. 

Summary

I'm not a developer/distributer/pro-gamer. I'm a consumer that has played games as a hobby. I constantly see the trend of when a title drops with alot of hype, everyone throws hate because they launched before a deadline. Alot are justified. This one is a rare case. It's beautiful, intriguing and absolutely mind blowing. A small example of where we stand in our own galaxy. Absolutely wonderful job to everyone that made/making this game possible. I'm excited to see where it goes. Everything has it's drawbacks, but give it a go. Especially while it is on sale.

TL;DR

Game so good wrote my first actual review. Put down some plastic, because this game blows your mind. Amazing game.

With the rocky launch and some (read; plenty) of broken promises, I didn't expect much from this game at all. After now putting almost 100 hours on the game I can safely say that it's a lot better than you'd expect.

The graphic style is slick and simple, yet captivating. The soundtrack is actually phenomenal, but it gets mixed in with all the blasting, lasering, jetpacking, flying and inventory-managing, so I suggest lowering the SFX and increasing the music for a bit, just to hear what the composers had to say.

All solar systems, including planets, moons, their surfaces, possible evolved lifeforms, plants and minerals, even their atmoshperes are completely randomly generated. This game follows a massive algorithm to procedurally generate a world with lakes, rivers, caves, deserts, beaches, forests, and some settlements, albeit repetitive ones. 

After the most recent major update, the game received some facelifts, and land vehicles. You can construct and upgrade your own roamer, a buggy-like car that can be drive underwater, a the nomad, which is like a hovercraft, capable of traversing above water with ease, and the colossus, a monstrous 8-wheeled tank with huge inventory space and power but not very fast. You can also equip all of these vehicles with turbo boosters, mounted cannons or mining lasers, and long-range scanners for locating rare resources, buildings or other points of interest.

The graphical options are varied but frustrating to switch since every tiny little change required me to close the game, launch again, load my save, tweak settings, rinse and repeat. But at least there are enough settings to make this game run on even some potato machines.

The game offers you a vast galaxy to explore, with a minimalistic story that you can either follow or ignore. The real goal is to explore the galaxy and make your own "YOU WIN" moments, be it by building a magnificent base near the galactic hub for many players to see, or by buying and fully upgrading a super powerful starship to raid trading freighters and haul cargo quick and safe. 

Now if you dislike managing a minecraft-like inventory in a game with dozens of different materials and resources, this might not appeal to you as much. I've spent hours just managing inventory space, and the game informs me with a "synthetic" voice about every action i do in the inventory, be it building an upgrade or crafting a piece of trade material. Even so, if this game goes on a good sale, even the most cynical space-enthusiasts should give this game a go. Who knows, maybe Hello Games manages to deliver all the wild promises that the game was hyped on. Eventually. In patches. We hope.

I think Hello Games was pressured (perhaps by Sony?) into hyping up No Man's Sky into something it wasn't. Prior to release, players were led to expect some ultra-ambitious space MMOFPS with a AAA budget and team - i.e., "Star Citizen Lite". Instead, what players got was more like Minecraft.

But, like Minecraft, No Man's Sky is incredibly fun on its own. Basically, you mine for resources in order to fuel & upgrade your ship to go explore the universe. What's rewarding is discovering a world with a beautiful array of plants and animals, beautiful planet-filled sky (all the more impressive with the knowledge you can actually travel to those worlds!), and watching the sunset over impressive landscapes. You can also build your own bases!

There are AI characters in this game. Aboard space stations or in small dwellings on planets you'll find characters you can trade with or hire. Sometimes space pirates will come attack you and you have to fight them off in a cool spaceship dogfight. Some planets have hostile life forms or robots too. Some planets are themselves hostile - extreme cold or radiation draining your life support system, which you'll need to recharge. Of course, there's plenty of opportunity to upgrade your suit & ship - or even purchase new ships. I haven't gotten that far, but I think you can even purchase your own giant freighter ships for extra storage space, which in turn can contain numerous smaller ships for exploring nearby solar systems. Overall, there are some pretty cool things to do in the game.

If you're the type of player who, like me, spent most of their time in Skyrim just wandering around and exploring stuff, you'll enjoy No Man's Sky. If you're the type of player who rushed through the quests and always used fast travel, it's likely you'll hate No Man's Sky because wandering around & exploring is what it's almost all about. 

One more thing: this game is NOT worth the full price of $60. Get it on sale for $20 or $25 at most. This is not a AAA title. It really is closer to Minecraft or Kerbal Space Program than it is to Star Citizen, so don't pay more for this than you would for either of those.

Reviews.173290:
[h1]Great game, horrible history[/h1] 

I've bought this game on two different platforms (Playstation 4 and PC/Steam). I've got the platinum on this game for PS4 and intend on doing the same on PC within a few months. I [i]understand[/i] that there were a significant amount of promises that just weren't kept at the launch of this game - it's left a horrible aftertasted in everyone's mouth when it came down to Hello Games and "No Man's Sky". HG has attempted to push to make NMS [i]somewhat[/i] presentable, post-launch. I realize there was a large period lacking communication, no updates, and radio silence from Hello Games in general. After a while, this eased up and we got both the "Foundation Update" and "Path Finder Update" - not at once, but after the silence was over they kicked development up into high gear. 

[h1]Find What You Like and What You Don't[/h1]

Aside from the marketing (and misleading statements [sic]), No Man's Sky is a pretty fun game if you go into it with a reasonable [b]self[/b]-driven expectation. When I bought this for PS4 at $59.99 - I only wanted an exploration/mining game that took place in space. Multiplayer in a game like this, for me, would be an annoyance (if HG ever does implement "full" multiplayer, please make sure it's in another mode outside of survival or regular). I didn't want to run around with friends, nor get shot at by someone random that's flying through space. I've played 500+ hours of EVE Online - that's more than enough experience with getting salty over a game that should be "chill". 

There's a little bit of everything in No Man's Sky - you can get creative in creative mode, you can test how long you can survive in survival, and so on. I enjoyed the main campaign - the hunt to keep yourself alive, while mining and crafting upgrades along the way, and trying to get to the center of the universe. Now that people know what's at the end of the universe, there's not many who's interested in such a thing - but they still exist (like myself). The point is - you can hate the game, you can like it, or you can find that it being on sale actually raises the dollar to value ratio for you.. whatever the case, you're free to believe what you will. You're free to meander around worlds or never buy this game. 

Personally, I recommend it to those who simply want to explore or create. Exploration can be tricky, at times, but worthwhile if you're lucky enough to be on a resource-heavy planet. If you want to create, creative mode does allow some liberty and doesn't throw you into the deep end.

I kind off just realised that the whole game is going to be this, mine ressources to upgrade things, keep exploring (your ship also needs maintenance) and then mine ressources to keep yourself alive.

I might just have been unlucky with my starting galaxy, maybe there are some amazing planets out there that could match the quality of some of the screenshots but I doubt it.

If you go into this game with 0 expectations then you may actually enjoy this game.

I think most if not all negative reviews are based on what this game DOESN'T deliver (due, in part to the hype created before release) which I do understand because gamers were blatantly lied to.

However, if you approach this game without actually knowing what the developers promised then you will enjoy it.

Its a GOOD game, If not a little repetetive, ( but then what survival game isn't? ) gather this, create that, refuel this, go to point A, gather that, go to another planet, open this, gather that rinse and repeat.

I am only 7 hours in and ive been to a couple of galaxys, maybe explored 7 planets ( not in their entirety ) and i'm beginning to enjoy what's going on. Meeting different races on the space stations, exploring the different worlds and renaming the worlds i've discovered. There's something rather satisfying about discovering undiscovered planets and seeing the differences. ( even if the differences are small ) Different planets have different lifeforms, different toxicity levels (if any) more or less aggressive lifeforms.

However, everything you do is reliant on you constantly mining, as far as i can see there's no getting away from that. To refuel your shuttle you need to mine, to create just about anything requires you to scan your location and go gather the resources you need. I don't mind grinding resources but if you do, then don't bother with No Man's Sky because you have to gather to do anything.

That being said the one major issue I have with this game is the actual mining itself, It feels like my eyes are being burnt out their sockets, It's so bright and "flashy" everytime I ore some iron or anything it's so unbelievably sore on the eyes and like I said, mining isn't a choice. No matter which filter I use (filters change your surroundings to different colours) It still hurts and there's no "brightness" option as such in the settings. I've never had to stop for breaks during games as much as I have in the last 7 hours.  

TL:DR

The game is good (so far) If not a little repetetive, Mining hurts my eyes as it's so unbelievably bright! 
Worlds seem slightly different but still feels worthwhile.

Do not buy this game at full price though, I got it on sale for around £15 and it seems about right pricewise, the last time I paid £15 for a game was when I bought Rust and I played 1300 hours, somehow though I seriously doubt No Mans Sky will provide that amount of entertainment.

Good game 7/10

I just got the game a couple days ago. Already 20 hours in and no bugs for me, yet.
Loving it so far.

The only thing I think it really, really needs is a manual or a simple tutorial to familiarize a new player with what they can do and how. Especially on Steam, where there's no physical manual that accompanies the games.

I was five planets in before I looked online how to scan animals and plants (f key). I figured it was something I was going to be introduced to through the tasks, but it never came up.
Also, how to switch from mining laser to blaster (g), and construction (z) and your discoveries (esc, and two pages over from the options and close game button).

I also looked online about how to find a habitable base and claim a home planet. Things I could already do, but didn't know I could.

Otherwise, the game is a beautiful experience that has a more early sci-fi feel to it. It's not another dystopian wasteland, but rather the planets evoke the works of Asimov, Bradbury and that generation of writers, and that makes it feel all the more fresh.
And I just discovered today that you can change the video filter for in-game play, as well. 

It does cater to a certain kind of player, though. That is those players that enjoy exploration and an immersive atmosphere.
Fortunately, I fall into that group. I could sit in my ship on an alien planet and watch acid rain fall on strangely colored vegetation for hours.
Or watch the sky shift from day to night, or vice versa.
Or sit in a space station and watch the ships land and take off.

And there's just enough conflict and threats with dangerous atmospheres, aggressive animals/plants, the drones and pirates that it does feel more lived in and not just a lavish walking simulator.
I think I've died three times so far.
The first two times were because I didn't know the nice looking drones go hostile if I mine near them.
The third time was when a group of pirates jumped me when I was flying to a planet.

And... I've learned to be careful in caves. Their safety and beauty hide the fact that you can easily get lost if you wander in too far. I spent a good hour just trying to find my way back out of one and watching my life support slowly go down. The panic set in once I realized that I was lost and if I died, I wasn't going to want to retrieve my stuff.

I also really love the seamless experience of walking on a planet, jumping into my ship, flying off into space and landing on another planet or space station. I swear I feel a bit disoriented everytime I start walking again after flying through space. 
It's things like that that make me like the game.

I'm actually kinda glad that I waited until now to get the game. I'm sure I would've hated it or at least been very disappointed back during launch.
But in its current state, it's much better than I expected.

To help me decide on getting it or not, I watched two separate youtubers as they 'came back' to the game after the recent updates: JustJarrod and VintageBeef.
After watching their videos, I reviewed Steam's return policy (as I've never refunded a game before) and decided I'd go ahead and get it since it was on sale, and I'd play it for an hour and decide.
When I finally decided to stop playing for a bit and make a decision, I was surprised to find that I had been playing for two hours.
And no time during those two hours did I think 'this is bad' or 'why did I get this'.
I was actually enjoying it.

My advice to anyone is that if they're considering getting it, go ahead and try it.
All the bad reviews are basically as over exaggerated as the hype was when it came out. Take them with a grain of salt, watch some recent gameplay videos and make your own decisions.

[h1] The Love/Hate Relationship [/h1]

[i] My story with NMS is huge.

Started on 2013 with the Hype train. 

Went through excitement with every trailer/teaser released. 

I expected the BEST space game ever, like a lot of people.

Turned out disappointed and angry.

Had to sell my PS4 back in the day. Got a cheap but good laptop gamer later.

Watched the community fall and rise from afar.

Stopped caring about the game after I got Elite Dangerous and Starbound.

Started to care again, after some updates but more cautiously.

Wasn't impressed.

Evolved my concept of gaming and evolved as a person too.

Don't get hyped or believe in everything easily again, thanks, Sean (no pun intended).

Got interested in the new Waking Titan hype.

Wanted to get the game but is expensive for me.

Got it gifted from a VERY NICE guy.

Started a new time... [/i]

[h1] The game [/h1]

No Man's Sky is an exploration sci-fy game.

It's very chilling and peaceful.

[h1] The Flaws [/h1]

I would once review the game as awful, truly. 

I still despise the marketing strategies and how Sean Murray handled things.

He should've put the game on Steam Early Access instead of on Sony's hand.

Although he got rich and now has [b] NO EXCUSE [/b] to not deliver the game he promised.

[h1] The Reviews [/h1]

People still hate NMS because of the bad RP they've done. Period.

[h1] What you do? [/h1]

In NMS you explore. It's not like Elite Dangerous where the main focus is combat.

Here you wake up after your ship crashed and mine resources with your tool to fix your equipment and ship parts.

In the meantime, you explore the planet you are in and after that, you can hop out of the planet to go to another one.

In exploring you scan animal life that can be uploaded to the servers for in game money too.

[h1] The Updates [/h1]

With the updates now you have:

1 - [b] Survival Mode [/b] - [i] My preferred mode. It's really challenging [/i]
2 - [b] Normal and Creative Mode [/b] - [i] Normal mode or creative (you have everything free to use and easy) [/i]
3 - [b] Base building [/b] - [i] Seems very cool, I haven't build one yet cause I'm playing on Survival [/i]
4 - [b] The rovers [/b] - [i] Cars to run around planets, which I will love to have. IMO they could be not base related cause I hate walking big distances on the planet [/i]
5 - [b]  Classes [/b] - Ships have classes now, which is cool
6 - [b] Freighters [/b] - Big ships stationed on space, dunno the purpose yet. They look like just rocks there for now, as I see


[u] This are the ones I recall [/u]

[h1] Where can it get better? [/h1]

1 - [b] Quests [/b] - [i] There are quests from NPCs but only to build bases [/i]
2 - [b] MYSTERIES [/b] - [i] My main complain in the past was the lack of mysteries to find on planets. There are the Ruins and Monoliths but I expected running into aliens in trouble or aliens wanting a fight or aliens in need of help or more than just crashed ships with generic messages but crashed ships leading to more things to discover. More under the sea things to do and see to and the list goes on
3 - [b] Black Holes, Worm Holes and Portals [/b] - [i] Make black holes do something cool like send you to a random system in a random galaxy OR implement Worm Holes for this and make the Portals active with something GOOD to do when you cross them. Portals could be the wormholes of the game IMO, like what was shown on trailers

[u] With more mysteries, for ME, the game would deliver [/u]

[h1] Overall [/h1]

7/10

I give 7 because now I enjoy the game from what it is, knowing that there is a lot do deliver yet. Has bugs and flaws like any big game but is enjoyable as a chill experience (even on survival).

No Man's Sky is a single player experience game by Hello Games.  There is no object of the game nor is there an end of the game.  The game is about exploration and survival in a procedureally generated universe.

There is no multiplayer.

There have been two major updates since the game was released in August 2016.

First came the Foundation Update which gave the game three different modes, Normal (the original game), Creative (same as Normal but but without worrying about resoures or player health; a sandbox mode if you like) and Survival (same as Normal but with more difficult conditions to be encountetred).

Next came the Pathfinder Update which added Permadeath (same as Survival but when you die, your progress is erased, gone forever).  It also added base building and three vehicles to aid in your exploration.  And a whole host of other graphical enhancements.  Also included in this update for PC players is the ability to share your base via Steam Workshop.  Another addition in Pathfinder is Photo Mode which helps the player take screenshots by giving the ability to 'move the sun', different filters, add or remove effects such as fog or cloud layers.

Though there has been no offical word, it appears that a third major update is in the works, possibly involving portals.

https://www.nomanssky.com/foundation-update/

https://www.nomanssky.com/pathfinder-update/

There is a passionate community around this game and also a passionate crowd of detractors.  I would not reccomend No Man's Sky to everyone but if you into chill games with no objective, I'd reccomend it.

I enjoy the game just for sheer beauty it can create, from sunrise or sunset to outer space or inner space, the graphics are simply beautiful.

Check out YouTube for people Live Streaming the game for an idea on how it looks, feels and sounds.

Happy exploring!

This is the thing.

No Man's Sky was a blowout failure of a title.

It was promised to be a top-tier game with endless amounts of fun and explorative excitement. This is simply not the case TO MOST.

The game has a lot of bugs that could have been fixed, errors that could have been righted, and marketing campaigns that could have told the truth. It features very little in terms of new and exciting ways to play and enjoy yourself.

That being said, this game is not a complete write-off. Expensive? For what your getting, yes, it is quite the hassle.

For some strange reason, I keep it installed. Maybe to put in a few minutes of fun times every few weeks, or maybe just because there's something special about going around a solar system's planets and space stations to encounter a billion new things everytime.

Throughtout the time I've played, I feel an almost absurd amount of curiosity and amazement for a game that seems to offer nothing to support it! Maybe it's the Relics scattered from lost civilizations and mysterious goopy substances invading the uninhabited wastelands of some planets. 

Maybe it's that one second, I'm swealtering through a barren wasteland with only two inhabitants, and the next I'm on a water-world filled with massive fish and flying whales.

Maybe it's that I just want to like this bust of a game, because it is the closest thing we have to exploring the stars like some of us dreamed of doing as kids.


~Pros~

-Great Graphics
-Wonderful Atmosphere(s)
-Fantastic Ship/Alien/Space Station design
-House Building
-Sound Design
-Control Scheme is simple

~Cons~

-Lied to consumers
-Expensive
-Poor post-launch support
-Suggestively simple resource-management
-Multiplayer is Disconnected (it does exist, but not in the typical fashion)


Now, after everything is said and done - I do recommend playing No Man's Sky. It's entertaining, keeps my attention for my exploration needs, makes me laugh, and does everything a good game should.

However, if you are looking for just a space exploration game, go check out Elite: Dangerous. It's far superior, just without the walking around bits. 

Overall? 

If it's on sale, pick it up. The time you enjoy spending in the Galaxy will far outweigh the problems that exist.


I hope this helps. <3

Before you look at my rating and go "hurr durr hello games are liars hurr durr". I would like to point out what I find good about this game, and also what can still be done to make it better.

With the new updates adding home bases, vehicles and freighters, the player's possibilities have ben drastically expanded. Now, this does not imply that the current content is sufficent, both in regards to this being an AAA game, and also because it is sold as a full game which it in no way is. Luckily we are seeing a development model similar to what Mojang are doing with Minecraft, meaning continuous free updates bringing more content to the game, keeping it fresh.

Now, what can be done to make this game better? First off, I want to point out a major bug that has rendered me unable to play the game properly. It has to do with teleportation from space stations, back to your home base. Personally, I would advise you to not buy the game until this is adressed, unless you want to make new bases whenever you travel to a new star system.

Another quirk has to do with the space battles. Sometimes when you enter a new star system, you can encounter a space battle where pirates are attacking a freighter. You can either side with the pirates and attach the freigher stealing their cargo, or you could help out the freighter and receive a reward from its captain. If you decide to side with the freighter, a single stray shot, hitting it or any of its allies, will turn it hostile, even though you are in the process of killing the pirates. Kind of like accidentally killing a chicken in Skyrim while saving the entire village from a dragon. A solution to this problem could be to turn the freighter and its allies invulnerable whenever you decide to side with them.

My final opinion of this game is, despite it's bugs and broken promises, positive. With their new development model adding fresh new content, I am sure this can turn into something great. I would, however, advise you to wait until some of the major bugs (like the teleportation one) are fixed before buying it, unless you want to end up as frustrated as I am.

In the midts of all the negativity of this game, I had decided to take a diffrent approach than everyone else. 

The biggest problem people have with this game is not the game itself per say, its the developers. They hold them responsible for the promises they made and never delivered on. But lets take a step back fpr a moment.

When I first bought this game, I had herd NOTHING about it execpt what I saw Markiplier and Jacksepticeye play on it. Yes, the $60 price tag was steep for me, but that was the price of nearly every big name game at the time, so I held it at the same level as the other games. 

When I first started playing, I was enthralled. I was loving the whole concept of the game. The multiple lange system that you had to learn each and every word for, the barter system, the space combat (albeit kind of lacking in enemy diversity),  and the ever changing planet terrain and weather.

After about 35 hours (Which is longer than the ENTIRE GAMEPLAY of MOST games coming out on the market today), I started to feel a sense of repetitiveness. So I looked up reviews on the game, and thats when I got swept away in the torrent of negativity. I critasized every little flaw could find and beratted the game because it was not what it was supposed to be.

But now, I have taken a step back and I realized something. I bought a game. I payed this price for something that came from someones mind. An Idea that sprang up and was turned into digital data. I have attempted to make games before before, and let me tell you, the complicated algoritms to even make 10% of a game like this function correctly is a level that I will never understand. Its a game, and for all its negativity, its well made. I found very little glitches. Its a fully explorable, 100% Free Roam environment space exploration game. Which is actually pretty cool. Its fully 3D, and in VR, this would really be something special, and its GIGIANTIC. It took me 41 hours to explore 3 galaxies. and only FULLY explore 1 of those. And that alone, is worthy of my time. Sure, a lot of the Textures are a little blocky and flat, but no game is perfect. and maybe thats just the idea behind it. 

I can argue all day with people about this, but this is my review. I give this game a positive rating because its a Well Put Together idea. I have no play issues. Everything flows smoothly. The game holds my attention and for all its bad hype, its a GAME. I have seen people pay a LOT more for a LOT less. I have seen people pay $70 for games full of bugs and compleatly incomplete. So I say, play it with an open mind and be honest to yourself. Its a game. I dont care what the developer diod or said. what I care about is the GAME and thats what I am reviewing. Plus, at least the developers are taking the critasism to heart and trying to make the game better. The newest release added a lot of new things to the game, so I say check it out if you want to. Anyway, thats just my opinion. take it as you will.

First things first, the game is too expensive and should probably drop to maybe a half. But do not underestimate what you get.

I want to look at the game now for what it is today, not for what people (rightfully) expected it to be a year ago. There have been huge updates that have added a lot of depth to the game. As somebody who was part of the "refund party" a year back, I gotta say many disappointments have been made up for. I am very certain that if the game was released in the state it is today, it would not have a "mostly negative" rating here on Steam.

Anyway, I like to compare this game to Minecraft in many ways. In my opinion, after the updates, this game should be liked by everyone who likes playing Minecraft as a solo player. The multiplayer is extremely limited in No Man's Sky (you can read messages from other people and visit their bases), but this was never my reason for wanting it.

Don't play this game if you want a purpose - there is none. You are being put in a (practically unlimited) universe and what you're going to do is up to you. While this was pretty bland walking/flying around in the beginning, updates have added reasons to go look for certain things and try stuff out.

The universe and everything in it is randomly generated and quite diverse - but of course there are "patterns". It will get boring after a while, but you will come back for more at some point and might experience some surprises after all. Maybe after weeks or months, but that doesn't really matter. Somehow I achieved my 120h in this game and there are still things I want to do at some point and I'm sure there's stuff I haven't seen. I am pretty confident by now that more generated content will be added in the future.

Of course, there is so much more room for good things. What's really lacking still is some kind of "lore" between the factions. Right now they just seem to co-exist, I hope that changes. Another thing is that you will get the same "rewards" for doing certain things over and over again. In my opinion, they should add something you would want to collect - like the artifact collections in Spore, or rare items like in The Elder Scrolls games that serve no real purpose, but you want to have them and place them in your home.

In conclusion, take the game as a space explorer without expectations or hype, and you will be positively surprised. The negative comments are mostly about expectations that haven't been met, and that is Hello Games' fault. The hype *did* fail. However, you still get a game that plays like an AAA title (good controls, very good ambient music layers, gorgeous visuals, even on my notebook that's way below specs) and there are a lot of nice things to do and see. If they keep working on it like they have been since the release (albeit very quietly), sky is the limit.

I always wanted a game like this, so I have to admit that I went into this game more willing to like it instead of just checking it out because of mainstream hyper or w/e, but I got to say that it's actually not that bad. I enjoy exploring planets, finding crashed ships and patching them up or doing "quests" for my recruited specialists. The survival part and base building part is not that much of a grind compared to games like ARK and as I said the overal space exploration theme just really speaks to me.

60 euros is still a bit much for this game though. It can offer hours of fun, but only for the people who actually really enjoy it. For the type of player who wants to just play it for a little while and move on again the price is just not worth it at the moment considering the content you get back for it. At the start you have very little inventory space, which I did not necessarily mind, but I can see how its frustrating for many others. Also I'd like to see more meaningful interaction with the different alien species. As I sit here on the train looking to get some work done, I am way more interested in listening to the No Man’s Sky soundtrack. I am a casual drummer who put his sticks down a while ago, I just haven't felt inspired, I guess. I just finished listening to the first 3 songs: Monolith, Supermoon and Asimov and already I'm inspired to get into music again. This is a fucking great soundtrack.

In my experience with the game, paying the money to be introduced to the music alone was worth it. Like most, I'm sure, I've been burnt in the past buying a game that I thought looked cool but had shit reviews. There aren't many times when I've bought a game with shit reviews and absolutely fucking loved it, but this is one of them. I figured that most of the shit had come from people at launch expecting much more than what was on offer feature and content wise than at launch. Fair enough. I picked up the game and played it for the first time on the 28th of April, and for me I'm in love. Loving the sheer scope of the universe, the color palette, the imagination behind it all and for me there definitely is sense of purpose. The game shows you that which, sounds like it wasn’t there before. It’s there now.

The music, fucking great. 

Anyway I learned today that not all negatively reviewed games are shit. I still have to be careful but the chance I took with No Man’s Sky was a win. I can't speak for you but this is my experience and based on that, recommended.

Cheers.

Reviews.173936:
TL;DR:  Buy on sale if you've played Subnautica to death and don't need multiplayer
Okay, let me get my can opener and open this can of Worm Soup that is No Man's Lie. 
First, context:  I bought it on sale after the Pathfinder update.  There's a lot of hate for this game that I mostly missed.
I almost bought it when it first came out.  I'm glad I didn't.
Second:  I've never played a crafting game before.  The closest was crafting professions in WoW like, 10 years ago.
So maybe other crafting games are better.  
But the real question:  Is the game any good?  I have played quite a few hours(much more than 4) and so far, I'm really enjoying this thing.  I understand the argument that finding new planets and new creatures and such would get old after awhile, but it just hasn't happened to me yet.  Combinations are still fresh to me, at least for now.  

The Good:
A lot of stuff to do(even if you factor in repetitive procedural generation, it still actually does have a lot to do)
Building a base is turning out to be very interesting. 
SOME of the game's promised  epic atmosphere is here... the starship fleets make a big difference even though I've steered clear of combat so far.  
The game is just complex enough that I needed to look some things up. 
I do love naming things.  Just, putting that out there.
Faction rep and base-building do give the game some sense of direction.  I don't want to reach the center until it does something more than reset. 

The BAD:
Lies, lies, and damned No Man's Lies.
Sometimes the game feels like Hoarding In Space Simulator 2016 V1.2
No multiplayer.  I'm dinging them for this because they said it would be there, but it still isn't.
I wish the ships had more direct controls.  I want to fly under arches and have the threat of slamming into mountains. 
Physics are not there.  The planets don't rotate, the moons don't revolve... the star systems don't have suns.  Day and night are just the sky changing when you're on a planet.  A bit of a cheap hack.  
This one will bring controversy:  Space is too busy and dense!  Unless the warp drive star map only shows systems that are both hospitable and too remote to be near cities, this doesn't really work for me... the planets should be further apart, and there are way too many asteroids and other ships.  This stuff won't really matter for a lot of people.  But I put a lot of time into KSP, so it leaves a bad taste in my mouth. 

RECOMMENDATION:  Absolutely!  If...
1)  It's on sale or used(do not pay $60!  $35 is okay)
2)  You've played Subnautica to death or are bored between updates(Subnautica seems to be the objectively better game to most people)... I guess if you really are dead-set on outer space instead of the ocean, this is a yes as well.
3)  You don't need the multiplayer(go with Astroneer or Space Engineers for that)
So I have to recommend, because I did get it on sale, I won't be playing Subnautica(seen too many videos of it), and Space Engineers and Astroneer actually seem more limited in scope.  
I would buy the game again knowing what I know now, no-brainer.  But only after the pathfinder update.  
I haven't even unlocked any exocraft yet.

And I've written the same long reviews I never read when other reviewers write them.  For shame.
