Reviews.173961:
Game purchased on sale (40% off), version 1.2 (after two big updates).

[h1] 'Disclaimer' [/h1]

N.B. this brief review will mainly focus on the game itself, and not the questionable behaviour of Hello Games and Sean Murray. I personally think Sean should have said something (f%$in anything!!?) after the PR sh%$ storm they received. That said, I think the hate against this game got a bit rediculous, and imagine at least 50% of negative reviews are mindless drones copying 'lies lies lies!!' cry babies. In any case, I agree that at release it's not worth 60 bucks, hence buying it on sale, and it still has some ground to cover in becoming the game I think most people want it to be.

[h1] My Experience [/h1]

I am absolutely loving this game! The visuals are beautiful (see my screenshots! [url=http://steamcommunity.com/profiles/76561198296647968/screenshots/?appid=275850&sort=newestfirst&browsefilter=myfiles&view=imagewall] HERE [/url]). The progression in character abilities and enhancements is really well executed. Contrary to popular opinion, I am finding tonnes of things to do in this game. E.g. just look at steam achievements, there's a 'todo list', if you're not into a complete sandbox (i.e. objectiveless) experience. While not perfect, the random generation algorithims seem to work quite well for me, and I am constantly met with new and interesting environements and situations to explore and experience.

In short, I think the game as it stands is well worth the sale price I paid, and certainly has the potential to be worth those 60 bucks.

[h1] Game Modes (mainly survival) [/h1]

I am not a particularly casual gamer, so at present I have stuck to survival and permadeath. I realise this is something that the original release didn't include, and so can forgive negative reviews based on the limited casual play; personally I like a challenge. I died twice on permadeath, then decided to just stick with my survival game until I reached the center of the galaxy (getting achievement), then there's some replayability on permadeath (different achievement), when I'm more of a vet explorer.

At the very beginning the game can be very difficult, but far from unfair as I've seen some people complaining about. As long as you plan things, make use of resources and learn from your mistakes, you should be able to pull through. E.g. if you head out into a blizzard from a cave and get past 50% frost protection without turning back, you are taking a risk, and cannot complain when you end up freezing to death being whipped by wild plants and animals.

I died a few times on both survival and permadeath, before getting my bearings with the game's mechanics and vital methods required to survive. Since then, it has only gone uphill for me. I love getting a new ship, a new power tool, new game changing abilities like vehicles (exocraft) and extra inventory storage (huge driver to improve). Initially it's a bit of a grind, especially with iron, but I see that as a necessary evil in order to really appreciate the progression and upgrades towards faster grinding, including grenades that instantly mine out an area of resources for you.

[h1] Random Generation (v1.2) [/h1]

So one of the biggest challenges this game faces is how to randomly generate terrain, items and biological organisms in a variety of ecosystems / environments, and make it look 'good'. I think we should acknowledge that this is a very non-trivial task. So I can excuse the odd c%$k up, and even enjoy them for the hilarious frankensteinien messes they are, big fan of [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-5jWtz3rzco] this vid [/url]! (cracks me up every time)

In my experience, the terrain generation is working wonderfully right now. Caves, valleys and mountain ranges feel natural in most places. I actually got lost exploring a cave system so extensive my life support ran out before I could get back out (lesson learned, unplanned caving ~ risky). The planetary flora is wonderfully varied in color and style; recently found a tree that appeared to be covered in anuses, named it 'Anusesgalore'! The fauna can be hit and miss, though on average feels quite good and decently varied in the stock parts used in random generation.

Though whatever I've said here, I advise you to go look at my screenshots (maybe small spoilers, but if you're concerned, just avoid reading any text)! They say it all (I'm an sc whore, especially in a game that includes a specialized feature to take photographs!). You may formulate your own opinion from these (and I imagine many others people have taken).

[h1] Pros and Cons [/h1]

So I'm now getting lil bored writing this, and I think you get my opinion of the game as it stands. I'll list some pros and cons from my perspective, then wrap up.

[b] Pros [/b]

[list]
    [*] BEAUtiful environments and creatures (with the odd failed genetic experiment).
    [*] Compelling races, characters and ongoing stories (e.g. quest lines with base characters).
    [*] Varied land and space combat, with multiple weapon styles and enemies.
    [*] Well designed progessional systems, keeping you hooked for that next upgrade.
[/list]

[b] Cons [/b]

[list]
    [*] PR fell into an abyss from day one.
    [*] Damaged reputation from what I would agree was a far less respectable version 1.0 (1.2 ~ much better).
    [*] Someone let Sean out of the programming room and into some interviews where his over excited imagination cacked everything up for them.
    [*] Though I think the game as it stands is wonderful to play, still feels a bit like something that's in development and pushed out way too early. The 60$ price tag was bs, and a terrible shame they didn't decide to cut it back a bit.
[/list]

[h1] Summary / Closing Remarks [/h1]

There's a lot more I could say about my experience with this game, though as mentioned I'm getting bored of typing this and it's that in general I reccomend getting it on sale, or even retail price if you think it sounds like something you'll really enjoy (probably is!).

I will say that one cool feature appears to be how you can name and upload things you 'discover', and get paid based on the 'importance' of the discovery. E.g. life forms typically make you more money than rocks :P. Here is where any 'multiplayer' currently lies, as you are able to see other people's naming of discoveries, and vice versa, and it's like you're part of a community working to map out and explore this randomly generated universe. Again, non-trivial problem, and I admire and am impressed at the current state of it.

Also, for opposing view at release, please see [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uTTPlqK8AnY] angry joe's take [/url] on this (probably my favorite game reviewer). I will say that many of the things he complains about have been addressed in the recent updates, e.g. when a milestone is unlocked, you have the option to quickly skip it if you wish.

Finally, my personal advice to anyone reading this and seriously tempted to buy this game: Ignore the negative reviewers, most of whom are jumping on a band wagon of trolls and haters; Look at [url=http://steamcommunity.com/profiles/76561198296647968/screenshots/?appid=275850&sort=newestfirst&browsefilter=myfiles&view=imagewall] my screenshots [/url] as primary source material on what things look like in the game right now, and make your own decision. Personally it took me a few days to weigh it up, but in the end I caved and I'm so glad I did!

I love aliens. My whole life I wished I could be the charles darwin of an alien planet, so I was sucked right in by the concept of No Man's Sky. I wanted it to be everything they claimed it would be, I wanted to love it! I wanted it to be the only game I'd ever play again. Unfortunately, It was very hard to like No Man's Sky. In fact, I hated it.

Never in my life have I regretted so strongly any other purchase, than No Man's Sky. Not only does the game fall short on almost all of its over-hyped promises, but it is incredibly over priced at a retail $60.00. The advertised "scale" of the immense world is only possible because the logorithmic creation of all of the planets and creatures produce cheap copies and knock offs that are boring, repetative, and uninteresting. The immensity of thier under-delivery makes Spore look like an incredible success by comparison. I sunk about 40 hours of gameplay into this, and after about 16 the patterns in the game are so blatantly recognizabgle, that any suspended disbelief comes crashing down on your head, and shatters the immersive quality.

The only joy I got out of the game was naming and categorizing the various species of the more interesting worlds (which were incredibly scarce and impossible to mark for return), and learning alien languages via an extremely grindy collection system. These are the most rewarding activities in a sea of pointlessness. This game is a sandbox, so directionlessness is to be expected, but in other sandbox games, there are unique and interesting story threads and hooks to draw you to the good bits, and you are rewarded for exploring them farther. No Man's Sky has no such story, only vague and shallow references to historic events that have no impact on the game play, or the static and stiff "characters" (if you can even call them that, as the only things you interact with in the game are dumb animals and vendor merchants).

To be fair, the engine is powerful, and the developers have broken a lot of ground with the way procedural generation can be used in games, and a lot of respect and credit is due there. The game is also beautiful. The bubbly and saturated aesthetic makes exploring very fun, and the style is detailed enough that you'll catch yourself admiring a lot of the flora and fauna. I took a lot of pretty screenshots cresting hills and looking out over crazy alien vistas, I even set my desktop backround as one for a while. It was a nice stress reliver after work to just fly around and name animals and take pictures.

Mechanically on the other hand, the game is lacking in some simple and time-tested necessary UI features. It doesn't even have a system of mapping or tracking the worlds you have visited, making it frusturating to find your way back to resource deposits or just cool sites. The game is very inventory dependent, and the tools it gives you for managing those inventories are counterintuitive and limiting, making you constantly feel like you're being punished for collection things (which i must stress is all you can really do in the game.) The gameplay is incredibly repetitive, and grindy, as you blast rocks to get resources to build things... that make you better at blasting rocks to build more things... that also blast rocks. The combat is easy to master and the enemies lack variety and challenge, not to mention they are basically a lore-less cop-out of designing a compelling antagonist. It feels entirely like an after thought.

All in all, the amount of time you have to sink into this game is immense, and the rewards are paultry and empty feeling (aside from building a ship, that was dope.) The story is weaker than hotel coffee, and the gameplay is akin to making cornmeal. A rating of 4 out of 10 would be generous, and its only because I respect the studio and what they have done here, not because I think the game experience deserves it.

Yes, we all know the hype, big promises, how the launch went and all those missing features etc. I did not jump in the hypetrain, I actually very much didn't like or even understood the core idea of the game back then. And I hated the style of the graphics.

But as a scifi fan, I followed the news and some mild interest started to form, nevertheless at the same time I was being sceptic. I was sure the game could not possibly deliver all those features they were talking about. Or could it? Well, after the launch when reading first impressions and reviews I was, even when not expecting too much, disappointed. A little surprised too, "Oh, it came out to be THAT bad?"

I was not going to buy this game. I have limited time to spend on games and these kind of games usually take a lot of it. No way I'm going to use my precious freetime to play time consuming, let alone bad games.

Then came the Foundation update. With base building. And survival mode. And I decided, for some reason, to buy the game.

And I'm very, very glad I did. Because it is almost nothing like I thought after reading all the bashing. I jumped right down to the deep end and started with survival-mode. Later I tried normal-mode and a brief test confirmed, that Survival is where this game really gives everything it has to give and all the well thought out mechanics and gameplay loops are in use. And this is important. Very important. In normal mode flying your ship is basically free, money and resorces come in faster than you can spend or store, you are constantly finding new tech, blueprints, bases... This means money loses its meaning. Exploring loses it's meaning. And for example rover is useless, why would you drive anywhere if you can fly there? You don't need to worry about plutonium, you literally stumble upon it everywhere you go. I can see that normal mode works for others, but I also see that it is part of the NMS's problem because it makes the game too easy and pointless. Fortunatelly, it all changes in Survival-mode.

In the beginning of the Survival you are constantly fighting for your life and low on everything. You need to plan your moves very carefully. At the same time you need to repair your gear and try to make your way to your ship and repair that too. It was an awesome experience, and when you are finally sitting in cockpit, ship repaired, filled up and ready to go, you really feel a great sense of accomplishment. But it does not stop there. Every take off needs a FULL tank of plutonium. So you need to carefully consider is certain place or planet worth landing. This is one of the things that greatly impact on the game experience on survival vs normal mode. You just can't proceed as fast as in normal because you can't land everytime you see something interesting on the ground. Also every new discovery feels fresh and instead of "discovered new place every other minute" there might go hours before you see a base, outpost or shelter of any kind. And that's awesome.

I remember this one time when I rushed to this small outpost, again just barely making it. Environment shield died a few seconds before I made it through the door and inside. There was one alien and he had cool looking multi-tool on the wall. I looked at it and checked the prize, whoooa, over three million credits. Bit more than my 200 000cr which I was able to scourge together so far. It would take a while to be able to buy that kind of stuff when I was barely keeping my self alive... I decided to talk to the alien before I go, if I was lucky he might give me some blueprint or something. I walked to communicate with the alien and he wanted to see my own, still basic multi-tool. Cool, maybe he makes a mod or something, but no. He took my multi-tool and gave me that 3000000cr badass gear from the wall! It came completely out from the blue. Right now I can't rember ANY game, where one single gift or loot from a npc has felt so special and expensive. I will always remember that encounter with that friendly alien.

Fight for survival continues, even with the working ship and cool multi-tool. You still need to search resources and if there is a poi somewhere nearby, it is more economical to just try to walk there. Lots of people say that when you get your ship fixed, game becomes boring grind. Well, I certainly did not find it boring, exactly opposite. Game just starts.

It is far from boring grind. I don't play this game to reach center of the universe as fast as I can. I propably never get there. Instead my goal is to get rich, build huge base, buy freighter and cool ships, learn to "tame" the game universe. Make it my home. I've allready established a small base and am now able to drive a rover. It is very fun thing to drive and makes exploring planets much easier. And using it is much, much more cheaper than flying with your ship everywhere. You still need to do certain things, like resource scans on foot, though. But now you can cover those medium distance trips easily and unlike with a ship, you can search and collect everything on the way.

Well, of course the game is not perfect, far from it. I've encountered some bugs, and the game has crashed two times, which is annoying if you have lots of unsaved progress behind. Graphics are very good, but style still divides opinions. Animals could be more diverse and landscapes too, especially caves. But every now and then you encounter some truly cool planets and vistas that are out of the "norm", same goes with creatures. Space flying is lacking and controls are very basic, allthough pretty fun after you get used to them. Space stations are pretty forgettable, but now they are attleast crowded. And I agree, game needs a goal and more content for those who can't make their own. But as recent patches show, Hello Games actually started to deliver, so far with high quality content.


I've now spent 63 hours in the universe of NMS, more than on average game, and feel confident to say that I like NMS VERY much. It is not the game that was hyped, but it is a great game nevertheless! Exploring new planets, finding resources, meeting aliens, building your base, hiring staff, it all is very fun and rewarding experience. But I cannot stress enough, at least for me the game truly opened up in Survival-mode, Normal mode just smoothes out all the nice little details and mechanics in gameplay, those details that really make the game fun, varied and challenging.

There is not a single "flaw" that makes No Man's Sky a "bad game" - the sum of want was delivered just did not add up to what was promised.

First of all, some of the features promised were not included at all: It was implied that you could meet other players (unlikely as it were in the wide universe), but that was disproven only a few hours after launch. No Man's Sky is singleplayer, no matter what it tries to pretend otherwise, and you will never meet any other living soul ingame. Also look at the third trailer in the top (the one with the dinosaurs) - did you expect some kind of natural-looking ecosystem like that in the game? Nope, there is not, this was all "staged" for the trailer.

Secondly, the UI - it was/is clunky to use. Landing and launching take some time during which you can do nothing, so hopping from place to place on a planet with your ship is more toil than anything else - imagine it as short unskippable cutscenes every few minutes. Yeah, fun. Also did you hope to fly only meters from the ground? Forget it - if you want to go lower than several hundred meters you need to land.

Lastly, the big selling point was the infinite potential of the game - each world procedurally generated, always something new... Unfortunately it is not - after a few planets the game gets a "sameish" feeling to it, sure the trees are blue now instead of red, and that critter has stripes - but essentially it feels like the very same content recycled over and over and over ad nauseatum.

So my verdict: if you can buy it for 10$ or so, you might get your money's worth for the few hours you might play it, otherwise best stay away.

This review is for anyone who bought and shelved the original game but is now thinking of starting a new journey following the release of the Foundation and Path Finder updates. The review is based on 200 hours playing the original No Man's Sky plus a further 80 hours playing the game with the Foundation and Path Finder updates. The original game was bought with full knowledge of the critical comments circulating at its release.

So, here’s a summary to start with: the updated No Man’s Sky is better than the original for anyone who relishes a challenge. And for those who don’t relish a challenge, or just want a spell of relaxing play, there is now creative mode.

The normal mode of the updated game is more challenging than the original game’s single mode. Hello Games has tweaked the rules of its galaxy, so some resources are more hard-to-find, others exist in different places to the original and some are inaccessible during the initial stages of the game. While it’s obvious that fuelling systems will be tougher if materials are more scarce, the tweaks and changes have bigger implications. Seemingly small changes affect play-style when, and because, they are part of a chain of dependencies.

Here’s one example. Plutonium is scarce compared with the original game. This makes gathering fuel to power starship launch thrusters, build shielding, craft warp cells or make bypass chips for quick profits more challenging than in the original game.

But it also affects some fundamental game-play decisions - such as whether to walk, drive in one of the new exocraft or fly and, if flying is the option, when to land. Given the significant plutonium costs involved in getting back into the air after landing, the scarcity of plutonium can make it tempting to just fly by after spotting, say, a ruin. But checking ruins is now more than just a tourist stop because aliens in buildings no longer teach words. Choosing not to land to acquire a new word conserves precious plutonium, but at the cost of, perhaps, being unable to crack a manufacturing plant's word puzzle that unlocks a blueprint. And cracking those puzzles is important because blueprints are no longer widespread.

Instead, there are nanites, dispensed in miserly quantities when found in places such as abandoned buildings. Nanites are the currency for buying some pretty juicy blueprints from technology vendors who are located in space stations. Vendors don’t stock a full suite of blueprints, however; instead, each race specialises in weapons or starship or exosuit upgrades. Prices are high and vendors will not sell unless the prospective purchaser has achieved a certain standing with their race. As Shakespeare might have said: “To land or not to land, that is the question”.

It’s not only that plutonium is more scare in the updated game. Titanium cannot be gathered without an advanced mining laser now. Iron is the new fuel for both propelling and shielding starships instead of thamium, so a jaunt into space to harvest thamium to replenish a survival suit is no longer the cakewalk it was. Thamium still exists in space, but it's spread much more thinly than in the original game. On the flipside, iron in space in big quantities does give access to building materials for a planetary base. It is worthwhile following in-game prompts to construct a base and recruit staff, such as a builder, since some valuable blueprints unlock in the process, including those to get started on cultivating plants for profit. Iron is also widespread in caves but the latest No Man's Sky appears to have removed cave-based carbon. Instead, caves house a new element called antrium. This is an ingredient for plant cultivation and making voltaic cells which are, in turn, needed to build planetary base components including exocraft and storage containers.

The new survival mode ratchets-up the tension a notch. Where the normal mode spawns a traveller next to a broken starship and perhaps on a benign world, the survival mode spawn point is next to a building that is, based on experience, 5-15 minutes on foot from a starship that also needs more resources to repair and launch than in normal mode. Given that survival mode also appears to spawn only on planets with an extreme environment, keeping both the survival exosuit and hazard shielding up-and-running is essential and tough.

It’s unwise to expect success in every survival mode game. Planets with caves and resource stacks on the surface that can be burrowed into for shelter increase the odds of reaching a starship and launching without demise. Death may not be permanent in survival mode – that’s for the new permadeath option – but dying does wipe survival suit content completely. Storing items in the starship is not a solution since the game allows transfers from suit to starship at ranges over which it is impossible to retrieve them.

Movement on foot in a harsh environment involves a constant trade-off between draining life support or hazard shielding fastest. Any movement drains life support. Running drains life support quickly. Using the jetpack drains life support quickly, too, so negotiating uneven terrain is costly. Pelting around using the original game's 'run-melee-jetpack' combo drains life support frighteningly fast and makes it potentially suicidal now. Dawdling in a harsh environment may serve to protect life support but leaves hazard shielding to be hammered instead and, while it recharges quickly in a building, it recovers slowly when sheltering in a cave.

A tip for survival mode: don’t relax after reaching and launching the starship into space for the first time. A pirate gang will likely be waiting. Making it into space only to be blasted back to the original spawn point, losing every material stored in the survival exosuit into the bargain, can be somewhat frustrating. Okay, loading a prior game save is a way out of that situation, but it does diminish a purist approach to survival mode.

One niggle with the original No Man's Sky was that starship and multitool slots were added singly. It was frustrating to spend time searching for a crashed starship only to find that it had one - or no - additional slots. Now, it’s possible to find crashed starships and be offered multitools that have way more than just one extra slot. The catch is that many of those extra slots are unavailable until unlocked (repaired) at a cost of tens of thousands of credits per slot. Until then, the slots are tantalisingly 'redded' out. All the same, it is a better approach than the original. Starships having a trade-in value and a class rating system are other good improvements over the original version of the game. 

And now for a conclusion at the end. Playing the updated game for the first time did prompt moments of frustration when tactics and strategies honed during 200 hours in the original title just did not cut it any longer.  Having learned how the new No Man’s Sky galaxy works the game is, for me, improved. The normal mode is more challenging than the original game’s single mode. Survival mode is intense and absorbing. Creative mode gives relaxing exploration. Something for everyone, then.

Let me preamble this by saying that I didn't watch any No Man's Sky pre-release videos short of the obligatory ones just to know what it was about. I didn't watch E3 interviews. I didn't preorder it, or played it until now (March '17) so that's the reason you'll probably find a distinct lack of salt in my review. Apparently the game had quite a bit of performance issues at launch and progression was much different before the foundation/pathfinder updates which have greatly improved its mechanics and progression gating.

No Man's Sky is pretty good, for an indie game developed by a handful of people, which is what I expected coming in. Mine resources, shoot a buncha robots, discover planetary bases, fly around, sell exploration data, all works and it's pretty fun. It's not a game to buy for its FPS mechanics, or for the space shooting, it's a game you buy as a massive time sink you come to time and time again, finding new planets, new resources, new weird looking pokémon, new sick upgrades to your gear and slowly progressing towards the nebulous path of either the Atlas or the center of the galaxy grand quests.

The latest updates have greatly gated progression and now there's this base building element heavily reminiscent of Subnautica where one will be able to hire specialists and unlock modules, crafting components, vehicles and gear, so there's always a crumb trail to lead you along. Inventory management is alright, and surprisingly deep in the form of upgrades that depending on their position next to each other will grant you bonuses, meaning inventory shapes are relevant, and one will always have the option to either salvage broken tech and spend a buttload of money in restoring them, or buying them new for a hefty credit price mark, or, more often than not, restoring some broken tech and swapping it for a new one later on.

Ships look cool, multitools look cool, creatures look cool (wouldn't mind a handful more of palette swaps though, some look too similir to each other on the same planet), all in all, having bought it after the Pathfinder update and at half the launch price (which I think is the reasonable asking price, it's not a 60€ game but very worth 20-30) I think this is a pretty cool game for an indie title that you should definitely try if you enjoyed games like Starbound or Subnautica. The galaxy map is a mess and keeping a record of your visited planets is a pain in the balls unless you write things down, so definitely a lot to improve there, but overall, I think it's worth checking out with an open mind especially considering the work the devs have been putting towards improving it from what it looked like a much more barebones initial release. 7/10.

Let's get a couple things out of the way first. Number one, this is going to be one of the most honest reviews you'll see on this game. I'm not a troll, I'm not a fan boy... I said I would buy this game when its price was lowered to less than $40 and that's exactly what I did for the experience alone.

Now, before I can discuss the various aspects of the game I need to address the elephant in the room and get past it first. 

No Man's Sky is one of the biggest lies that I've ever seen. Don't get me wrong, this wont affect my review, but it needs to be said. Sean Murray is one of the most deceptive, and despicable developers I have ever seen. He blatantly lied on national television, online, etc about features in this game that don't exist (even now many months after release). It's why the dev team is/was being investigated in the UK for false advertising. Don't take my word for it, search "No Man's Lie" or "One Man's Lie" and you'll find all the evidence you need.

That said, below is my review of the game. If you want a shortened version, just skip to the final verdict at the bottom.


[h1]Overview[/h1]

The game throws you onto a planet and giving you a waypoint to your crashed ship with very little else to go on. You have a mining tool, probably a failing suit to the environment (acid rain, cold, heat, etc), and need to struggle to survive while repairing your ship. Once repaired, the galaxy is your limit. There is absolutely no hand holding here, it will be a struggle (on survival mode).


[h1]Graphics[/h1]

This game is visually "beautiful"... but also extremely ugly at the same time. Looking at planets and walking around them looks amazing. The effects looking around and flying are fantastic. But the ground textures are EXTREMELY blurry, planets look one way in space and as you get closer change drastically. AA effects are choppy, and animals look almost made out of clay. There are some significant graphics issues with this game that takes away from the experience (even when maxed out).


[h1]Storyline[/h1]

This game features an almost non-existent storyline. You get a main questline to obtain recipes... but it's not very up front and doesn't really do anything to tell a story. You don't understand these new races, and don't feel like you're apart of their struggle. You never find out why you're there, or what you were up to. You don't get a grasp of the galaxy and how it's laid out and just move from one system to another to eventually get to the center (which, the outcome is absolute trash and swift kick in your pants).


[h1]Side Questing[/h1]

There are a LOT of side things you can do in this game, not really quests so much as "give one of -these- to an alien" who in turn gives you reputation or recipes. Or learning a language word from one of three races. Reputation does absolutely NOTHING for your character or the story. You can't pick sides in a conflict, and you can't change your destiny based on your interactions. The interactions have NO effect what so ever on the galaxy. Once you've collected all of the recipes and brought a cube, or isotope to an alien, it just repeats. Completely repetitve and boring.


[h1]Combat[/h1]

General combat is fluid and fun. The worst aspect about combat is currently what should be the most important... space combat. Design flaws exist that really have me scratching my head (like the fact that in the middle of a dogfight I need to open my inventory and manually repair my ship while still flying and fighting). No hotkeys, no hot bar, nothing. Incredibly frustrating. Ground combat involves fighting drones (sentinels) or aggressive animals. Pretty bland, but smooth enough. You can pretty much avoid all sentinels by sprinting away from them. They give up looking for you even when standing in an open field in front of them.


[h1]Skills, and Upgrades[/h1]

No skills to be had unless it's an upgrade to your multi-tool or ship. Very little in the way of character development and if you find a new tool or ship, that's your instant gratification. Upgrades are crafted, which can be frustrating for people who just want to explore and not grind (farm). Getting ships is also a chore, or expensive depending on how you obtain them.


[h1]Game Performance[/h1]

I run a PC with the following specs:

AMD FX-8370 (8 core CPU) @ 4.01ghz
G.Skill RAM 16GB @ 1600mhz
Asus GTX 1080 8GB
Windows 10

I can run the game at 30-60fps on 1920 x 1080 with the graphics settings maxed out. Generally I get about 30fps on the ground and 60fps from the air. Which when you look at the blurry textures, the HORRENDOUS pop in (which I've crashed more than once into a cliff face because of how slow the terrain pops in), short viewing distance, etc... I should be doing a lot better here. I absolutely blow this game away with my specs and yet, it struggles. Definitely in need of a significant optimization pass, even though this game launched as a FULL retail release. Not an alpha.


[h1]Final Verdict[/h1]

This game is fun for ONLY two people. Casuals who want to explore and just fly around. Second are hardcore fans. These are guys that stuck with the game from the beginning and don't mind the grind (they'll also defend it with their last breath and probably even vote this review down). But if you're a survivalist, like space games, etc... there are other options out there for you. This game is NOT for you. With the state of the game, poor performance, and other annoying development decisions... I have to downvote this game. Even after the Pathfinder and Base Building updates. 40+ hours into the game and I'm unimpressed. 

This game should have done two things... been classed as an Early Access game from the start and been priced at $30. I´ll try to be brief. 
You´ve probably already heard all of the negative sides, that the devs didnt deliver what was promised, no multiplayer ( cant recall it being advertised as multiplayer.. ) etc. There are plenty of reviews about that, so I´ll try sticking to a little bit of both, and let others solely bash on it.

The initial game was somewhat lacking in its content. Visualy beatutiful, but lacking in depth. Now was it because of the console-release being rushed, or the hypetrain blowing things out of proportion? No one will ever know, probably a little bit of both, but the game had a lot of potential. 
Unfortunately I think the window of opportunity has passed and the game will never be more than "what could´ve been"

Still. I cant help to  commend Hello Games for standing fast trough the insane amount of heat they got, and for continuing developing the game, pushing patches, not just fixing a few bugs and call it a day, but actually fixing stuff, plus adding content. ( a lot )

In my experience there are plenty of bigger, established developers that treat their game/fanbase a whole lot worse, and wouldnt  spend a second on further developing a title that got a fraction of the negative feedback that No Man´s Sky got.
And if so, they would release it as an paid expansion..

In its current state ( Path Finder 1.23 )  the game runs a lot smoother, looks more vibrant and plays very well.
One can tell they´ve spent time on making the additions to the game look amazing and detailed. Also the numerous small  things, as item classes, additional responses/stories to conversations, playmodes, shortcuts,vehicles, bases etc etc. The list actually goes on a fair bit, and all of this really adds to the gameplay.

Is it perfect? -  of course not. Will it ever be?  - Probably not, but it isnt nearly as bad as unplayable/unjoyable as many seem to portrait it like, just becaue of all the pre-launch hype, making a lot of people dissapointed/angry.

Now, keep in mind that I´m a casual gamer. I dont do 12h straight sessions, making my experience with the game last a lot longer. 
So I can suppose if I did, it may  feel a bit shallow without a deeper story and [spoiler] an ending that just loops the game.[/spoiler]
I enjoy it immensely as a relaxing game, playing it in "creative" and just take my time freeroaming the vast universe it offers. 

So my conclusion:
[list]
    [*] Is it a bad game?  - No, not even close
    [*] Could it be better? - a lot of things could, including this game
    [*] Is it woth buying for 60$? - No, even tough I like it, I wouln´t pay that amount again happily.
    [*] When should I buy it? - If its on sale, and you are the kind of person that like an open universe exploring game, but can do without elaborate story and depth.

Here is my experience which I have right now with the game and with Steam:

I was asking for refund after 10 hours (and 7 days) (my first refund) - REJECTED. Well done. Steam is platform for awkward indie games, support for anything more complex is limited. Embarrassing.

- Basebuilding again - After you build a base you should move to next sector towards galaxy center. Weird? Yes it is. Why to stick to one place when I need to go forward ? Nonsense. Moreover, when you build new base on next place, previous base is cancelled, and all refinement you bought is lost, except some material. - Crafting is good element for survival games. This game is not survival and the crafting is not done very well. You need to gather resource A. Then create a thing B, add another thing and craft C, add another thing and craft D, and finally craft product E which you need for hyper-jump. Confusing in the beginning, boring afterwards.

- Confusing is also inventory. You have space ship inventory and personal (suit) inventory, both are very limited. It gets full on 1st or 2nd planet. Since then you are always looking into inventory what to purge, but you don't know what thing is important, what to keep and what not. Just pick some trash at random. You can't drop it, you can't store it somewhere else, you have to delete it.
- You cannot craft, buy and usually talk with full inventory. Next ship with 3 more space costs around 300.000 of something. The best ship around 10-40 milions of something. It will be long way to the galanxy center...

- Aliens, common 2 types. Frogs and Lizzards. No movement, just sitting / standing. Stup1d.

- The nice thing is sunset / sunrise on different planets.

Somehow I have managed to clock more than 600 hours into this game. Does this make me biased? 

You would tend say it does, but instead I'd like to think it made me more critical of what the game is, and isn't. 

For an exploration game, I'd say it is without a doubt the biggest game I have ever played regarding playing field. It's full of planets and moons which you can explore to your hearts' content, but space is depressingly empty. Once you've seen one asteroid field, you've seen them all.

The adding of freighters in the Foundation patch livened it up a bit, but the game could definitely use some more anomalies, rogue star bases, system wars and space battles.

Planets and moons are awesome. Graphics wise this game can be mind stunningly beautiful. And if you're like me, someone who could just wander around enjoying sights and views, you're in for a great time. 

However, play long enough and you'll start to see the same trees, rocks, and even similar creatures, wherever you go. Play a while longer and you'll start wishing they'd add more parts, and be more giving regarding size limitations, and density. 

Underground planet exploration is disappointing, you can explore caves upon caves, which are richly generated by the game, but you won't find anything worthwhile in them.

Storylines, quests, npc interactions, are nice, but at one point the storyline becomes a somewhat semi-tedious journey, the quests run dry, and the npc interactions are recycled. There are no repeating quests or jobs with rewards worth spending time on. 

The Path Finder patch added one repeating quest which will yield you some credits, but when you're at the point where you can do it you could just shoot a few creatures, create some products, and end up with a bigger monetary reward.

So why you might ask have I given this game a thumbs up, and why did I spend so much time playing it?

Everything is procedural, and I love it. It's a game where you can go and do anything you'd like to do when you want do do it, as long as it's within the game's limitations of course. 

I am unsure what to expect from Sean Murray and his team in the future. I do not regret buying this game for the full price, but I did need a long break before the first patch as I was just burned out on the lack of depth and content.

Recent patches made things better, and if they keep this up, I'll definitely keep playing.

I played this game for 94 hours. Is that enough for you? This game is a multi system simulator that specializes in procedural generation. If you look for an MMO first person shooter, then go play your Call Of Duty, idiots!

This game offers:
1. Open universe to explore with impressive attention to details.
2. Survival gameplay.
3. Craft, improve and repair your suit, spaceship & multi-tool (gun, bomber, scanner, resources collector).
4. Find technologies, resources, languages, loot, goods, weapons, spaceships, land stations, space stations, aliens, space anomalies and more.
5. Text adventures.
6. Trading, buying and selling items.
7. Massive freedom with variety of gameplay options. There is no goal! You are lost in space hoping to survive. Feel free to play and experiment with everything.
8. Fight animals, wild plants, sentinels, robots, space pirates.
9. Different game mods and a special crafting mode.
10. Each free update adds so many features like: vehicles, buildings, crafting, resources, technologies, plants, music, animals, alien interactions, more content and fixes then you could imagine! I still want action and adventure, but I don't want to feel exhausted after playing, especially if I've already had an exhausting day in the real world!

I don't know how my feelings about the game will change as I progress, but right now I am LOVING it.

Reviews.174288:
OVERVIEW
No man’s sky is a procedural survival sandbox in which your goal is to make it to the centre of the Euclid Galaxy. Masking a complex algorithm of procedural generation is a relatively easy survival experience with simple mechanics that still offers depth for those that are inclined to create their own adventure. For some, the quest to reach the centre is enough to make the journey worthwhile. For others, it becomes little more than a mindless chore to get there. I fall somewhere in between.

1ST TIME PLAYING
I love the thought of being the captain of my own starship, to go where no one has gone before and discover worlds at my own pace. However, the centre of the galaxy taunted me with it’s mystery, and for the first 50 hours of gameplay, that was what dictated how I played the game. I fell into a pattern of only landing on planets if I absolutely had to. I upgraded to a ship that I was comfortable with, bought fuel for my hyperdrive at space stations and kept hyper jumping towards the centre until it was engrained into my muscle memory. I eventually grew bored of the grind and stopped playing.

2ND TIME PLAYING
The Foundation Update that added base building intrigued me, but not enough to bring me back. It wasn’t until the next update, the Pathfinder Update, that I decided it was time to get back into the game. This time around, however, it wasn’t about finding out what happens at the centre of the galaxy, but to explore the new features of base building and land vehicles. Even though Hello Games have been kind enough to allow old save files to work in the new updates, I decided to start over.

This time around, enough had changed for the game to feel fresh, more vibrant than before. Not only the visuals had been updated, but the mechanics and gameplay felt more refined. My goal now became to find a suitable planet to build my first base on. This proved to be a much more difficult quest than reaching the centre of the galaxy, but still rewarding in a way that the grind never was. I enjoyed the game a whole lot more now than at release, because I had a sense of purpose other than finding out how the game ends. For me it was enough to know that I was on my way to finding out, and that I would get there in due time.

THE STORY SO FAR…
I eventually found out what happens at the centre of the galaxy, and I wasn’t disappointed.
I never did find the planet I was looking for, but I’m sure I will.
There’s 18 quintillion planets to choose from.
One’s bound to be perfect.

+ Infinite
+ Procedurally generated
+ Base Building
+ Weapon and Ship Upgrades
+ Freighters with multi-ship parking

~ Grindy

- No Multiplayer (YET)

SCORE
Story: 4
Features: 6
Gameplay: 8
Graphics: 8
Sounds: 7
Music: 9

TOTAL SCORE: 7

As a late comer to No Man's Sky (just got it with the Pathfinder update/sale) my first impressions are "Wow!  What an amazing game... but I'm glad I waited!"

Pros - 
::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::

What NMS does, it does VERY well.

The vastness of the game and scope is truly amazing. I'm a little over 40 hours in, just got my third ship, and is there SO much more to do. Yet it feels like I've done so much already.

I've encountered a Toxic mushroom layered planet, a breathtaking blue-sky'ed white fluffy clouded desert planet, a tropical island paradise with a beautiful ocean, a rad-infested wasteland of bizarre looking plants, two separate ice planets, one with deep caves, the other with a frozen ocean, dozens of outposts, trading posts, abandoned factories, monoliths, etc.  I've mined mountains of gold, and buckets of plutonium, and found a hauler crashed on the previous mentioned desert planet, fixed it up and claimed it as my own.  I've fought space pirates, defended freighters, and took out bounties.  I'm almost max rep with the Korvax, and getting there with the others.

And I've done all this with only exploring about 200 square light years... in a galaxy that is hundreds of thousands if not million times bigger.  The sky is the limit for opportunity for adventure it seems.

The graphics are insanely good.  Every planet has vistas of pure artwork.  Just looking at a planetary system in space is like something out of a sci-fi movie.

The physics are really good.  Ships are easy to control, and getting your character around on-foot is pretty much effortless (unless you don't watch where you're going).

Base building is SO intuitive and easy to do.  It is simply amazing how they made it all snap together seamlessly.  And the quests you get from the station workers frames an interesting story, and gives you a good bit to do.

The story so far seems fairly engaging.

Cons - 
::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::

All that being said... What NMS doesn't do, it doesn't do right at all.  And I completely get why people were insanely salty when this game came out.  There's a lot that was not properly advertised or communicated.

The interface leaves something to be desired.  Not being able to transfer items from the Exocraft to your player inventory is a silly and unnecessary inconvenience.  Having some keys un-mappable is poorly done (like being able to change the transfer key from X to something else).  Having to constantly manually recharge shields in space combat is clunky, and takes what would otherwise be a decent arcade style combat and turns it into a menu click fest.

The resource grind is REAL (I've been playing on Normal at that too).  Managing an inventory to the degree you have to in NMS is a major buzz kill.  But... I do see how that becomes a part of the game.  That being said, base storage is kind of a joke and needs a re-think (how about more slots, but with 250 stacks?)

Not having multiplayer - well... that's a whole can of worms I don't care to dive into.  I know it's a major source of contention with the Pre-release crowd.  I just hope they fix it without creating some BS subscription plan thingy.

There are still some crash bugs in the software (I've been kicked to Desktop twice).

There is also some definite repetition to the planets and creatures.  You can tell that algorithm doesn't skew things up too much.  And how come every star system has a Space Station that’s immense in size... yet the races of the galaxy don't seem to have homeworlds or cities.  Suggestion for improvement would be to add these 


Conclusion - 
::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::::
No Man's Sky is actually pretty fun if you take it for what it is.    The procedural scope of such a huge galaxy is mind-blowing.  In that regard, it’s a technical triumph.

This game is definitely a steal when it’s on sale.  I might actually say it's worth full retail price.

So, with that, I give it 8/10, and do recommend it.

So, not to jump on the band wagon of outright hate for the game I wanted to give a fresh perspective at No Man's Sky since it's recent update Path Finder (Patch 1.22-March/2017). I have never played No Man's Sky and, thankfully, I was skeptic about the hype surrounding the title prior to its launch and never bought it. I picked it up recently on Steam at a discounted price for about $32.00. 

After about 50 hours of game play I feel I gave the game it's best shot to win me over. However, those 50 hours were not, for the majority (and unfortunately) fun. I kept playing hoping for a better outcome, but No Man's Sky just kept becoming more annoying and frustrating to play. 

The UI and controls were heavily designed it seems for controller and a lot of it just doesn't make sense for practicality or ease of use. 

(Warning: There are a few parts that are really bogged in detail and I suggest skipping them. It’s there if you really want to read more on the subject and feel my frustration pertaining to the topic at hand. I will highlight when it is done with a big FINISHED at the end). 

(SKIP – Inventory mess)
For instance, the vehicles with the Pathfinder update inventory do not transfer to the character, but to the ship and there is no choice for either or. Usually between items transfer between the ship and character holding down a button for a brief second. However, to transfer items from the character to the vehicle, you go to the vehicle menu screen, hold down a button, search through a menu (of both the ship and characters inventory) to find the item you wish to store. However, you may run into an issue where an unstacked item in a character slot that is stackable in either the vehicle or starship becomes frustrating to stack since once you place the item in said slot (and are out of remaining items) you cannot continue to stack said item and are stuck with it unless you decide to delete something to just stack the item.
(FINISHED)

The lack of inventory management bogs the game down horribly. Also, a theme I can see from reflecting on my gameplay experiences is that there is a lack of control for the character. It feels like you are controlled as to how far you can go or how far you can do this or that. It certainly does feel the game is designed to make the player run constantly back and forth from a location for various reasons. For a game about freedom, there is not a whole lot of it.

(SKIP – Controlled Experience)
Want to explore? Wait, you need to stop and get “X” and “Y” resources or wait to recharge your hazard shield. That’s a cool looking building, you can blow off certain doors, but not these because you need “Atlas Passes” which can be found from rare encounters with Atlas crafts that are found in various galaxies that require “X” and Y” resources and “Z” recipes you find over the course of the game to reach them. And once you reach them you need to meet arbitrary in game achievements in order to unlock the next part. It may also require a few visits in order to get a pass at all. So, when you do explore without these passes, you visit a base and can only push one or two buttons instead of more which give varying degrees of rewards. 
(FINISHED)

There is also a sore lack of control for space flight and flying on the planet. It is super frustrating to want to stop, slow down or go faster when the game just stops you or just completely takes over control over the spacecraft. There were multiple times I threw my hands up in the air in frustration to let the aircraft figure itself out. And this is even found during space combat which is made abhorrently bad due to the lack of control and maneuverability that the player SHOULD have. 

(SKIP – Flight Controls and Space Combat)
Nose diving to the planet will about 120 mphs, but at top speed on the planet’s surface its 148 mph. Your spacecraft is capable of flying 1400 mphs, but the game won’t let you. Now this could be due to terrain generation or terrain detail as you fly over, but I feel it’s a lame excuse. And, yes, you can go into the atmosphere to fly faster over the planet to reach a point on it, but I hold my complaint firm because of how slow it is to enter back into the atmosphere. Also, the game the will not let you crash. You can’t hover neither in space or on the planet’s surface. You are constantly moving 30 MPH. 
(FINISHED)

The upgrade system is also horrible. Upgrades that are additional do no stack or replace, so your already limited inventory system will be bogged down with upgrades that you wish to keep. And if you want to replace an upgrade, like heat protection for cold protection, there is no way (that I could find) to store an upgrade. You either delete it or you don’t. And some upgrades just don’t work or are so little they are unnoticeable. A vehicle upgrade stated “+100% maneuverability.” I got the upgrade; drove around for a couple minutes of stress testing, deleted the upgrade and found nothing changed. Nothing.  

(SKIP – Upgrading gear and vehicles)
Here is another example why the upgrade system is bad, I found a water planet and wanted to explore it. (Also, out of fifty hours of gameplay I only found one water planet and the rest of the planets had zero water sources on them; IE no lakes, rivers, waterfalls, nothing like that.) I built an upgrade to explore underwater, but it lacked any UI interface to tell me how long I have to breath. I had to keep pulling up the inventory tab and to find out that I had about twenty seconds to mess around before I had to come back up. The next upgrade is just an additional twenty seconds. If I want to stay down there, I would need to bring as much of “X” resource as possible to continually recharge the device by pulling my inventory, press the resource or device and to recharge…constantly every twenty seconds.
(FINISHED)

The game is still riddled with countless bugs and crashes. It is clear with the pathfinder update and related objects. It feels rushed. Everything about this game needs to be polished. It doesn’t need more content it needs to fix its foundation first. It’s a great idea, but poor execution. And these continued updates of content are appreciated (and why I bought the title), but the abhorrent amount of bugs and frustrating mechanics in place make for a horrible experience. No Man’s Sky has a lot of potential, but I feel it needs to be completely remade. It is not worth $30.00 and certainly not worth $60.00. I am not a person who feels game play per dollar amount equals a good value. I feel a good game is what pertains to a good value. I would easily pay $100.00 for a fantastic game that was only a few hours long versus a game that was poorly made but could be played for thousands of hours. I bring this up, because I want No Man’s Sky to be good, but it’s just not worth it. It is so frustrating to play and it is just disappointing because they have something there, but ruined it. I am going to continue to follow updates for No Man’s Sky, but I am not going to hold my breath.

Story time! I come out of a jump, right into a pirate battle as they're praying on a helpless freighter. I can attack the pirates, attack the freighter and raid for supplies while they're busy with the pirates, or just fly away. I decide to be the good guy and dog fight the pirates. When it's all over... the freighter captain offers me a reward, or to sell the freighter at a steep discount. I buy the freighter, giving me tons more inventory and I find out I can even use the basebuilding system inside.

Some time later the same thing happens again with an even bigger freighter... After so many pirates that my ship barely limped into the docking bay, the discount is so steep that, with trade in, it costs me nothing. Now I have one of these: http://i.imgur.com/cUigV57.jpg Ready on command to follow me anywhere I might go, bristling with turrets and with a fighter patrol to fight off any of those pesky pirates.

--

Recommended if you're experienced in the genre and have a good idea of what you're getting. It's a fun game with many neat things to find when exploring, good to play at more meditative pace. More details below, but especially if you're new to this genre, I recommend watching an LP/Streamer play it a bit so you, as said, know what you're getting.

--

The core gameplay is not too different from those like Starbound or Terraria (especially early Starbound, when you had to worry about temperature and such). Run around a planet, hit stuff with your mining laser, craft stuff, and work your way up a progression chain of what you can mine and craft. But you do have to watch environmental hazards and your life support meter. A lot of progression content is also quest gated.

If you like the survival crafting genre, overall it's a good game with a fair number of rough edges: notable number of bugs but *usually* nothing gamebreaking, and occasional crashes. It looks very nice and provides vast areas to explore, with the usual caveats of procedural generation (namely, sometimes it can feel same-ish).

The basebuilding very heavily resembles Subnautica (minus power management), and even the exocraft (land vehicles) somewhat take after the tiers of Subnautica's crafted vehicles -- so if you've played, it will feel very natural to you, but it should be intuitively simple even if you haven't. It's overall very good.

A lot of people are saying that Hello Games were pushed by Sony to release this game early. If that is true, they would understandably stand to lose a lot of ground with a AAA developer/publisher if they even hinted at this. I think everyone knows they oversold and underdelivered what I think is a game that will likely live up to MOST its promises. Eventually.

If this had released initially with the coveted Early Access tag, this game would have been a shooting star of a game. But the above issue, coupled with what is admittedly TERRIBLE PR on Hello Games' part, did the initial negative reaction no favors (if no communication or patches for literally months after publication could qualify at all to be called PR in the first place).

So why should anyone pick this up now? Well, actions do speak louder than words. And in a world where talk has become increasingly cheaper, what's important is being communicated solidly. The patches that have since started to release are high quality, fix bugs, and address community concerns. The developers seem intent on delivering on their promises, if we can be patient. 20th century patient.

A noteworthy improvement recently has been transportation, which I think everyone would agree is key to a solid exploration game. They have added land vehicles, as well as freighter ships you can store your other, smaller ships in. They all handle rather well, though the game has a built-in purposefulness of actions that will take getting used to. Oh, and learn to Melee + Jump to boost!

And when you're not adventuring you can build a base on any planet and make that your home planet. I even liked the addition of teleporting between your base and any space station throughout the universe. This way of always anchoring you in the great expanse ends up adding a sense of purpose woefully lacking in the initial release. You don't get disoriented and it's fun to "go home" once in a while.

They've also fixed controls and made UI enhancements. There's permadeath and a few other modes as well, but I've decided to stick with my initial save file for now so I can't comment on those, my apologies.

I'd argue at this point, this is worth probably 30 USD if you were thinking about getting it before and put it off due to the bad release. 20 or less on sale otherwise. Honestly, we all kinda know what this game was initially going for. I know what we got wasn't quite... there. It's not going to be all of what was intended, but I think we're going to like what we end up with. They have a LOT of money to use to fix this thing.

EDIT: Almost forgot. Can't play with friends directly still. We won't be able to. We can share bases through Steam Workshop and technically you CAN visit them if you can find the planet. Good luck with that. Your friend won't be home. You can use their stuff though, so that's neat. Skyrim doesn't have multiplayer, but we deal with it I guess.

I held off on this game after release, only to buy it now (on sale) and find out that it’s pretty much what I hoped it would be. This is what I wanted from the game, and this is what I got:

1)	Light on story, but heavy on exploration
2)	Scanning, mining, gathering, salvaging, repairing
3)	Survival elements, but nothing so heavy handed that it feels like a survival game
4)	Cool space ships you can build or trade for
5)	Resource management
6)	Interesting creatures and biomes
7)	Impressive land to orbit transitions, with many planets and space stations to land in

This game (as is) is for casual players who simply want to escape into a different world, see crazy things while working on getting a bigger and better space ship. It is not Star Citizen (but good thing that game is coming!) but more of an SC-lite version. I personally did not expect any amount of multiplayer from NMS, so what we get (names, base sharing) is enough for me. I also really enjoy the art style, can’t wait to get back into the worlds and explore some more.

This is definitely a family friendly game, and one of the first I will play with my son.

EDIT: For those who think I'm not allowed to review a game after casual play? Guess what? I am totally allowed to, and this review is for people who will appreciate the game casually as well. 
I will never understand someone who puts 400 hours into this (or another) game and then downvotes it. That's far more absurd than my review for obvious reasons. I'm just giving an impression of the things I experienced and enjoyed, and how they are sufficient enough for me to want to continue playing. Even if I stop playing after 15 hours, as long as I'm satisfied with the experience it's enough.

This is the "Spore" of 2016.  A game that promised way more than it could deliver.  An open universe where you fly from world to world, star to star.  Planets with unique ecosystems, some barren, some brimming with life.  Man that would be a great game.

If planets have animals they're going to have somewhere between 5 and 15 varieties ... on the whole planet.  For plants it will be less. There's no concept of biomes at all.  Once you land on a world and spend a minute walking around, you can leave, you've seen everything the planet has to offer.  If that's all there is, making a huge planet is just a waste of time, why bother?

Furthermore there is a remarkable sameness from world to world.  Once you've seen a cave on one world, you have literally seen every cave on every world.  None of them are inhabited.  Certain key resources (platinum, zinc, "thamium9") come from flowers (for some inexplicable reason) and the flowers pretty much look identical on every world.

The creatures you come across are depressing.  Rather than creatively designing rules that evolve creatures for the environment they are in, instead the game seems to simply roll dice and create unrealistic chimeras by combining parts of earth animals "deer head, cat paws, antlers, ..." etc.  Nothing seems particularly unique to No Man's Sky and once you've encountered a few creatures, you'll note that the "toolbox" of "creature parts" is pretty small.

Worlds don't appear to be inhabited by intelligent life as you might expect... there are no "cities" or "towns".  You will occasionally come across a shelter that might have ONE alien in it, but no evidence of any sort of indigenous intelligence or even small settlements.  Interactions with aliens boil down to multiple choice questions.  Get the right answer and you might get a few resources or units of currency--but no sweeping arc of any grand story is affected by your interactions.

The controls are bad, particularly the flight controls, oftentimes you have to try to land your ship without being able to see what you are landing on, or fight in space without being able to see what you are supposed to be shooting at.  A number of interface decisions in the game are just downright wonky (on the PC version anyway).

Ultimately this appears to be a thin veneer of a game that can't possibly measure up to how it was billed by the makers.  You can probably get a few hours of fun out of it but the novelty wears off real quick. You wouldn't expect a game which takes an entire galaxy as it's setting to be far far FAR less detailed and immersive than say "Skyrim" but it is, and that's just sad.

For the amount of entertainment it offers, the game would be appropriately priced at $14.99.  I picked it up on sale for $35, and that was still too much money.  If you are desperate to try it, my advice is wait.  It *will* be selling dirt cheap some day, there's just not enough here to warrant anything more.

I figured No Man's Sky had gotten a critical beating, but they've had two major content patches, and it was on serious sale. I'd take a chance on it for space and planet exploration.

First attempt, well, there's almost no guidance on "normal" mode. I ran out of charge on my mining laser almost immediately, and the only way to charge it is with plutonium, which, well, I couldn't pick up now, because I was out of mining laser charge. Went to start a new game. . . .

. . . couldn't find a way to start a new game. Because there isn't one.

Alt-tabbing out to read up on the game on the internet caused a black screen crash, had to restart my computer, check my drive for errors, get back in, do some research. . . yeah. There's no way to start a new game. In fact, to restart, you have to delete your only available game requires going into the bowels of Steam and conducting file necromancy. (Yes, there's a 'go back to an old save' option buried in the options menu. I found that later. It's right next to 'exit to desktop' which is a story I'll get to in a minute.)

I sighed, and downloaded it to my son's machine, told him it was similar to Minecraft and Starbound, and he could try it once it was installed, via my Steam library. Except, yeah. Wouldn't even start on his brand-new laptop.

I sighed again, and figured I would kick it around a bit in creative mode.

I played for about 20 minutes. Tried to lift off into the sky to look for a space station. Promptly couldn't get my ship out of warp, and oh, look, no directions to on do so. Grabbed my phone, because I knew that alt-tabbing out to conduct a web search was a no-go. No directions online for *basic ship controls* that I was able to find--all kind of directions for upgrading ships, but basic controls that should have been covered in a tutorial? No.

Reloaded to an old save, built a save point, saved properly, and tried to exit the game using the actual exit to desktop command (which, as I noted before, is buried in the Options menus). . . and promptly got a black screen which dictated that I had to crash my machine again. 

So. That's pretty much the end of that game for me. Glaring bugs that crash a pretty herky machine, horrible user interface (lack of basic game utilities, like saving and exiting that function?), and no tutorial or documentation. Strike three, you're out. Which makes me sad, as I wanted to give it a real chance.
Reviews.174456:
Like many others, I watched this game before actually bothering to purchase. Gaming is now often done on a budget and we all want to get the most for our buck, so I'll make this quick:

Pros:
-Massive potential for exploration.
-Immersive gameplay and unique species with unique personalities. (Some even help you gather items if you feed them.)
-Dozens upon Dozens of vehicles, as well as ships in a variety of classes. Unlike most space exploration games such as Elite Dangerous, or EVE online, you can actually just find ships on planets and take them for your own, provided you gather the materials to get them fixed.
-Bases, Outposts, and Community areas, Oh my! (You can spend your entire time in this game on a single planet and still manage not to get bored, I keep finding myself wishing I could just stay on each world I visit indefinitely, but sadly, I yearn to see the stars more.)
-Easy controls (I have spent 3+ hours just trying to understand the basic keyboard and controller setups involved in a variety of space sims, never mind mastering the actual flight itself. In No Man's Sky, you don't have to have a yoke or joystick to be a flying ace.)


Cons:
-There is no jump system. By that I mean if you are to try and gain altitude, it is only based upon the thrust your jetpack generates. (Ironically, exovehicles have a jump.)
-Scaling issues with the RNGs will leave you with some creatures that are not  proportionate, to the point their existence in a world with the physics being portrayed could even support. That said, the fact there is variety somewhat makes up for this.
-Inventory is a crucial element in a space exploration game such as this, when you're going planet to planet, star to star, the fact you cannot have multiple ships with multiple inventories is a major let down, ideally I'd like to see some manner of orbital base one can craft to hold their potential ships in the future if possible, though the fact you can buy freighters somewhat makes up for this.
-Trade networking could be a bit more advanced, perhaps even offer the option to trade items for others instead of working simply off the premise of currency exchange. I feel some NPCs would require materials, much like I often find myself needing. Rather than trying to sell and buy off each other, I'd like to trade and increase my standing with other species in the process, though this would mean finding traders looking for the particular item you were hoping to sell.
-Fleet Dynamics can be a bit sluggish, or even dimwitted at times, you will rarely struggle to take on a ship provided you're willing to dive back into orbit for a few seconds to avoid sentinels. I would like to see the fleets break formation, actually maneuver and try to run / defend themselves rather than just sit in orbit like a space station.

Over all, I encourage you to try this game, but if you are hoping for a game where everything is exciting, you will be let down. There is a fair amount of monotony in this game, though like many games nowadays, grinding towards a goal is commonplace. There is fighting, but it is few and far between at times. You may find yourself provoking animals simply to get some manner of challenge out of the map, Just make sure you bring enough fuel for your life support, and you'll enjoy yourself rather thoroughly in this game.

As someone who affectionately reffers to this game as "No Man's Lie," I find it strange to write this positive review.

Looking back on just where this game came from, it's certainly come a long way from launch. Sean Murray's shitty marketing gave procedural generation a bad rap, and people fell off the hype train as soon as we discovered that it would be impossible to see another player. (If you had half a brain though, you'd notice that no open world multiplayer game could ever be paused) 

So with that, we left the game to the depths of steam hell, abandoned along with several other unrecognized titles of assumed equally garbage value.

But I always had hope for NMS. The game has it's fair share of bugs and glitches, but so did any title that EA or Ubisoft came out with. And NMS is a more original IP than most things either of those companies come up with these days, not to mention that their dev team is smaller. 

I want to make it clear, NMS is ART in video game format. That's not praise, it's categorization. Because the game just FEELS like art. Why do I say that? Well, some things that NMS and most art have in common:
-Beautiful
-Relaxing
-Meant for only the observer, i.e. the singleplayer experience
-Has little value to someone who doesn't appreciate it, and vice versa
-Can be viewed again and again, for hours at a time, and the awe is hard to cease when you do appreciate it

NMS is a chill singleplayer experience. That's all it is, and I feel like that's all it will ever be. Many people expect this game to roll out with multiplayer, and I for one know that's not happening. However, it doesn't need it either. Many people think that a vast galaxy should be explored with friends, and I for one agree in some regards, but this game doesn't play by those rules. What it needs is more content, but for a small dev team to work tirelessly against the current of the bad marketing that the game was born with to deliver the user free content, is actually very impressive. 

So, why would you want this game? In some ways, for the same reason why you might want Farming Simulator or Euro Truck Simulator, this is Artsy Space Simulator. You will buy this game because you want to come home from a day of your friends at school calling you a stupid queer for no reason, and just relax. Let your frustrations out on hostile space pirates and towers of resource deposits. Build your unique base and ride around the surface of your planet in your new rover. Or just fly around and explore, because the Atlas is a never ending quest that you will chase for ages. 

While the possibilities are not limitless, the sky is. The repetitive nature of NMS will last for some and die out for others. I recommend this game because I still believe in the future that it could have. If it dropped its price tag down to $35. Don't buy this game at full price ever.

Honestly, the biggest gripe I have with this game is the marketing and expectations set by Hello Games as compared with reality. This game will be forever rememered in many gamer's minds as a lesson about the dangers of hype, pre-orders, and advertising in general.

I do not and probably will never regain trust for Hello Games, Hello Labs or even Sean Murray, as these entities have blantantly lied and falsified information about No Man's Sky to the point I would consider criminal.

This game would be considered fantastic, innovative and exciting had the game been sold as a $10-30 (even 30 is feeling very generous) early access title. The flora, fauna and planet random generation combined with the ability to catalog and "discover" these new forms brought a breath of fresh air into the "survival" genre. I felt like an early renaissance explorer going from planet to planet claiming these new forms with my name along with the name I chose to give it. I put a good amount of effort in the nomenclature of my new creatures, bringing in latin roots and clever puns, imagining someday someone coming to my planet and appreciating the effort I went into classifying the bizarre alien world. The smooth transitions from planet to space were amazing and was one of the trademark looks from the very first peaks at the game.

Once a few hours were put in and the novelty wore off, the true shaky framework of the game become readily apparent. Ignoring the graphical and performance problems that seem to pervade AAA games nontheless, the 'features' that Sean Murray had gamers shitting their pants in excitement for turned into mere tricks to give the illusion they existed. What do I mean? I will give some examples.

Lets take multiplayer for the easiest example. Hello Games was very clear that you could run into people while exploring, but it was 'very unlikely' due to the sheer vastness of the universe. Shortly after the game was released, there is a video of two streamers meeting at the exact spot, yet they could not see each other. Sean Murray and Hello Games change the goal post of what they mean as "multiplayer", but now its readily clear there is no fucking multiplayer.

Beyond that, the controls flying around the planet feel like they were coded in an hour tops. The algorithm for generation started to show as features became familar and repeated. The "end" of the game was [spoiler]  just finding a hole and seeing credits.[/spoiler].( I put a spoiler there just in case, but just a hint it isn't that great). Fighting is elementary and the core game is just a big grindfest. I could go on, but there are many good videos out there that show all of the promises they made versus what it really is.

Oh, and that feature I loved where it recorded who found and named the flora/fauna/planets? Didn't even fucking save when I came back a few days later.
